articles.abstract: Patients with severe anterograde amnesia have been described as "stuck in time"; their mental time travel abilities are altered, and they seem to live in the present. Here, we examine an unusual phenomenon in which severely amnesic patients recurrently report the belief that they have just awakened from an unconscious state. A famous case illustrating this phenomenon was that of Clive Wearing who repeatedly wrote “I am now awake” in his diary. This unique cognitive phenomenon has not been specifically studied until now. We report three new patients who described similar subjective experiences. All three patients suffered from autoimmune encephalitis and showed massive bilateral hippocampal inflammation causing severe anterograde amnesia. We propose to call this phenomenon “Stream of Consciousness Impairment”, a reference to William James’s theory according to which, normally, we experience an uninterrupted flow of consciousness. This condition should be added to the spectrum of neurological symptoms that contribute to the study of memory and consciousness in humans.

articles.title: “It’s Just a Dick pic”: (Cyber)Rape Culture and Victim Behavior Predict Perceptions and Responses to Unsolicited Genital Images
articles.authors: Rocío Vizcaíno-Cuenca; Adrian Scott; MONICA ROMERO SANCHEZ; Hugo Carretero-Dios; Fiona Gabbert
articles.abstract: The unsolicited reception of genital images is a prevalent phenomenon, yet the influence of online social norms and victim behavior on judgments surrounding these incidents remains underexplored. In two studies with social media users from the United Kingdom, we examined how victim behavior and acceptance of myths about cyber-sexual violence influence victim-blaming and perceptions of incident severity. Study 1 (N = 131) found that participants attributed more blame to the victim and perceived the incident as less severe when the victim had previously chatted (vs. not chatted) with the perpetrator. This effect was only present among participants with higher acceptance of cyber-sexual violence myths. In Study 2 (N = 202), a similar pattern emerged, with the victim perceived as more blameworthy and the incident as less severe when she had shown sexual interest (vs. no interest) toward the perpetrator before the incident, particularly among participants with higher acceptance of myths about cyber-sexual violence. Moreover, we found an indirect effect of perceived sexual consent on this relationship. Our findings highlight the influence of online social norms on judgments of cyber-sexual violence and emphasize the importance of education on online sexual interactions.

articles.title: Beliefs versus Reality: People Overestimate the Actual Dishonesty of Others
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Helge Thorbjørnsen; Hallgeir Sjåstad
articles.abstract: Do people believe that others are similarly, more, or less dishonest than they truly are? The accuracy of dishonesty beliefs is not only important for psychological knowledge, but also has implications for organizations and policymaking. In this paper, Study 1 presents a research program on moral decision-making comprising 31 different effects from 11 experiments, where participants could anonymously lie for personal gain. Crucially, participants were also asked to estimate what percentage of other people would lie in the same situation. An internal meta-analysis summarizing all belief-behavior comparisons revealed that people substantially overestimate others' dishonest behavior (g = 0.61; k = 31; N = 8,126), by 13.6 percentage points on average. This effect holds across study contexts and participants’ own behavior, and 63.5% of participants overestimated dishonesty by 5 percentage points or more (only 25.4% underestimated it). We then examined potential consequences of biased dishonesty beliefs in three pre-registered follow-up studies. Study 2 (N = 981) found that providing correct information about actual honesty levels enhanced general prosocial expectations (e.g., trustworthiness, fairness). Study 3 (N = 285) revealed that professional managers have pessimistic beliefs also about people’s real-world dishonesty (e.g., insurance fraud, workplace theft), and moral pessimism predicted greater support for freedom-restrictive countermeasures to reduce dishonesty (e.g., surveillance). Study 4 (N = 741) demonstrated that providing managers with correct information about actual honesty levels causally reduced their support for freedom-restrictive countermeasures. In conclusion, the pessimistic bias in dishonesty beliefs about others is robust, and it shapes prosocial expectations and policy preferences.

articles.title: On the misuse of prediction in NeuroAI: A case study of Centaur
articles.authors: Jeffrey S Bowers; Guillermo Puebla; Sushrut Thorat; Konstantinos Tsetsos; Casimir Johannes Hendrikus Ludwig
articles.abstract:
In the field of NeuroAI, many strong claims are made about the similarity between artificial neural networks (ANNs) and the human mind.
A recent study by (Binz et al., 2025) is a case in point. The authors transcribed a large database of psychological experiments and fine-tuned a large language model to predict human responses on a trial-by-trial basis. This model, Centaur, outperformed domain-specific state-of-the-art cognitive models. We highlight several major problems with Centaur. Through simulation, we demonstrate that the model is not subject to basic cognitive constraints and that its behaviour is best characterised as a form of role-playing. More generally, we discuss the inferential fallacy of mistaking predictive power for explanatory power and the importance of subjecting models to experimental manipulations to test specific hypotheses. These critical points are often overlooked in NeuroAI, but need to be addressed if the field is to progress.

articles.title: Covert imitation acts as an adaptive reflexive gain control system in non-native speech perception
articles.authors: Hannah Wilt; Bronwen G. Evans; Yutong Ye; Patti Adank
articles.abstract: Current accounts posit that heard speech is covertly imitated to optimise speech perception. Behaviourally, covert imitation is measured using the stimulus-response compatibility (SRC) paradigm. In a speech SRC task, participants produce a prompted speech syllable whilst perceiving a speech distractor that either matches the target response (compatible condition) or does not (incompatible condition). The degree to which the distractor is covertly imitated is captured by the automatic imitation effect, computed as the difference in response times (RTs) between incompatible and compatible trials. Two theoretical accounts disagree on whether whether covert imitation is enhanced when speech perception is challenging or instead when the speech signal is familiar to the listener. To dissociate between these two accounts, we conducted two experiments utilising the speech SRC task (Experiments 1 and 2) and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) (Experiment 2) to evaluate covert imitation of native speech sounds (perceptually easy and familiar) and of non-native speech sounds (perceptually challenging and unfamiliar). In Experiment 1, participants performed an SRC task with native and non-native sounds, before and after receiving perceptual identification training with the non-native sounds. Automatic imitation was enhanced for non-native sounds compared to native sounds and decreased to a greater extent for non-native sounds than for native sounds following perceptual training. In Experiment 2, participants passively perceived native and non-native speech sounds whilst receiving single pulses of TMS to the tongue area of the primary motor cortex (M1). Tongue M1 showed higher excitability during passive perception of non-native sounds. Our results highlight that covert imitation is enhanced during the perception of perceptually challenging, unfamiliar speech, suggesting that covert imitation acts as an adaptive reflexive gain control mechanism to optimise speech perception.

articles.title: Social Disconnection is Associated with Impaired Social Skills: Evidence from Behavioral Performance and Automated Facial Expression Analysis
articles.authors: Vladimír Ivančík; Valentína Cviková; Sára Majsniarová; Natália Čavojská; Jakub Januška; Alexandra Strakova; Sebastián Petreje; Julia; Alica Hujsová; Radoslav Lošonský
articles.abstract: Social disconnection, consisting of loneliness and social isolation, is associated with many adverse mental and physical health outcomes. However, relatively little is known about whether social disconnection is also reflected in observable social skills. The present study examined differences in social skills and facial emotional expressions between socially disconnected and socially connected healthy individuals. A total of 107 adults were classified as socially disconnected (N = 53) or socially connected (N = 54) based on established cut-offs on measures of loneliness (UCLA-3) and social isolation (LSNS-6). Participants completed the High-Risk Social Challenge Task (HiSoC), a standardized behavioral assessment of social skills, while facial expressions were analyzed using automated facial expression recognition software. Social skills were evaluated by independent blinded raters across three domains (Affect, Odd Behavior and Language, and Social-Interpersonal Skills) and an overall performance rating. Socially disconnected individuals demonstrated significantly poorer performance across all social skill domains and received lower overall performance ratings compared to socially connected individuals. These differences remained significant after controlling for depressive and anxiety symptoms. In contrast, no significant group differences emerged in facial emotional expressions. Exploratory analyses revealed that greater expressions of sadness were associated with poorer social skill ratings, particularly among socially disconnected participants. These findings suggest that social disconnection is reflected in observable social behavior and may represent a distinct interpersonal vulnerability beyond general psychological distress.

articles.title: Patients’ and clinicians’ perspectives on a transdiagnostic Experience Sampling and Ecological Momentary Intervention protocol
articles.authors: Adam Kurilla; Daniel Dančík; Radoslav Lošonský; Alica Hujsová; Sebastián Petreje; Julia; Valentína Cviková; Sára Majsniarová; Petra Brandoburová; Anton Heretik
articles.abstract: Experience Sampling Method (ESM) and Ecological Momentary Interventions (EMI) are promising tools for person-centered mental health care, yet evidence on prolonged transdiagnostic monitoring remains limited. This study explored service users’ and clinicians’ perspectives on the usability and clinical utility of a prolonged transdiagnostic ESM protocol with on-demand EMI content. Within the DISCONNECT project, 84 service users completed debriefing questionnaires following a 30-day protocol with three daily assessments. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 service users and 10 outpatient clinicians. Data were analyzed using content analysis and thematic content analysis. Both stakeholder groups perceived ESM as acceptable and clinically valuable. Participants reported increased self-awareness, improved understanding of symptom patterns, and enhanced opportunities for psychoeducation, treatment planning, and patient–clinician communication. EMI was viewed positively but used infrequently. Participants emphasized the need for personalized assessments, flexible schedules, individualized feedback, and context-sensitive interventions. Key barriers included monitoring burden, clinician time constraints, and organizational challenges. Prolonged transdiagnostic ESM monitoring appears feasible, acceptable, and clinically meaningful, although successful implementation will require greater personalization and integration into routine care.

articles.title: oREV-VN: An extension of the oREV vocabulary test with Rasch-compliant verb comprehension items
articles.authors: Manuel Bohn; Chiara Carraro; Eugenia Rykova; Julia Christin Prein; Natalia Gagarina
articles.abstract: Research on early language development requires high-quality open access instruments to assess individual differences in early language abilities. The oREV is such an instrument to assess receptive vocabulary in three- to eight-year-old German-speaking children. However, it has been limited to nouns. In this paper, we report on the addition of a verb items to the oREV. We constructed a larger initial item pool and collected data from a large sample of children (N = 567) in the target age range. We used data-driven item selection to select Rasch-compliant items which were added to the existing test to form the oREV-VN. There was a strong correlation between performance for verbs and nouns and the combined task showed good reliability. The oREV-VN is freely available via the following link: https://devpsy.web.leuphana.de/orev-vn/.

articles.title: From Car Affinity to Risk Awareness: Understanding Driver Profiles and Shifts in Fatal Five Concerns across West Yorkshire, UK
articles.authors: Ibrahim Ozturk; Phoebe Pitcher; Rosie Revell; Neil Hudson; Esko Lehtonen; Gustav Markkula; Samantha L. Jamson; Natasha Merat
articles.abstract: Road traffic crashes persist as a significant global safety issue, with risky driving behaviours, commonly termed the “Fatal Five” (speeding, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, distracted driving, careless and reckless driving, and not using seatbelts), continuing to contribute to crashes and fatalities in the UK substantially. This study examines the relationship between driver demographics, attitudes toward driving, driving exposure, and drivers’ perceived level of concern regarding other drivers’ behaviours (in comparison to three years ago) in West Yorkshire. Data were collected from regular drivers (n = 669) and analysed using non-parametric tests and latent class analysis. Overall, distracted driving and careless and reckless driving emerged as the most concerning behaviours, whereas seatbelt non-use exhibited minimal perceived change. Compared to men, women reported that other drivers’ careless and reckless driving, distracted driving, and drink and drug driving are of greater concern. Three distinct profiles of driving attitudes were identified: Car-Positive Utilitarian, Car-Positive Experiential, and Car-Sceptical. While the profiles were mostly similar in terms of demographics, the Car-Positive Experiential profile was more prevalent among men and was more concerned about seatbelt non-use. These findings contribute to understanding drivers’ perceptions of other drivers’ risky behaviours and how driving attitudes relate to these perceptions. The results particularly highlight certain behaviours, such as distracted driving, as future areas of concern in shaping road safety interventions and enforcement strategies.

articles.title: Self-Coherence as a Higher-Order Organizational Process:  Toward an Integrative Theory of Selfhood
articles.authors: Laura Barca
articles.abstract:
How do individuals remain themselves while continuously changing? Contemporary psychological theories have primarily addressed this question through the concept of self-regulation, emphasizing the processes through which organisms adapt to internal and environmental demands. However, adaptation alone does not explain how individuals maintain a coherent sense of self across bodily, relational, and developmental change.
The present paper proposes a theoretical framework of self-coherence that integrates insights from embodied cognition, predictive processing, phenomenology, identity research, and constructivist approaches to personality. Within this framework, self-coherence is conceptualized not as an additional self-construct, but as a higher-order organizational process through which embodied experience, identity processes, personal meaning organization, and self-regulatory mechanisms are dynamically integrated across time. Embodied processes provide a foundational sense of continuity, identity supports the integration of past, present, and future experiences, and personal meaning organizations are reinterpreted as strategies through which continuity is maintained despite change.
Building on this perspective, the paper distinguishes self-coherence from self-regulation. Whereas self-regulation supports adaptive responding, self-coherence concerns the preservation of continuity and intelligibility across experience. Regulatory processes are therefore understood as mechanisms serving a more fundamental organizational task: maintaining a coherent sense of self over time.
By positioning self-coherence as a higher-order organizational principle, the proposed framework offers a conceptual bridge between embodied, developmental, phenomenological, constructivist, and predictive accounts of selfhood, providing a unified framework for understanding how continuity is established, maintained, and restored across change.

articles.title: Construct validity evidence for a Workplace Well-Being Questionnaire Battery adapted to Workers with Intellectual Disabilities (WWQBID)
articles.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles.abstract:
Background: Workplace well-being determine job retention among people with intellectual disabilities. No validated instruments exist to measure this construct in this population. This study aimed to validate a battery of questionnaires developed by an expert committee based on JD-R model, DISC-R model, and recovery theories.

Methods: The instrument assesses four well-being indicators, job characteristics, and recovery experiences. Administered to 169 workers in French sheltered employment, data were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis, McDonald’s Omega coefficients, and correlations to examine psychometric validity evidence for the questionnaire battery.

Results: Results provide robust preliminary evidence of the instrument's psychometric validity. Despite removing three items to optimize model fit, construct validity and reliability were confirmed. First evidence of concurrent validity was supported by significant correlations aligning with theoretical expectations.

Conclusions: The three-item dimensions for job characteristics require refinement to ensure validity. Future research with larger-diverse samples is essential to consolidate these findings.

articles.title: On Bias in Detecting Bias: A Signal Detection Analysis of Attributions to Gender Discrimination
articles.authors: Marie Jakob; Anat Shechter; Jimmy Calanchini; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles.abstract: Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of Signal Detection Theory (SDT), with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers’ ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers’ judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical SDT analyses of attributions to discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1 to 3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2 to 4) inform observers’ response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1 to 3), which reflects observers’ determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing.

articles.title: Mega-analysis of the Interoceptive Accuracy Scale (IAS) Structure and its Dispositional Correlates
articles.authors: Ana Neves; Magdalena Pfaff; Robyn Emily Scharte; Raquel Nogueira-Arjona; Giulia Poerio; Dominique Makowski
articles.abstract:
Traditional interoceptive questionnaires show poor convergence, suggesting they tap distinct
constructs. The Interoceptive Accuracy Scale (IAS), developed to separate accuracy from attention, is increasingly popular but psychometrically underexplored. Using a mega-analytic approach across 17 datasets (N > 33,000), we present the most comprehensive evaluation of the IAS to date, covering its factor structure (Study 1) and dispositional correlates (Study 2). Study 1 triangulated results across multiple dimensionality-reduction algorithms, identifying a stable 14-item core organized into 7 distinct item pairs linked to bodily sensations (e.g., Hunger–Thirst). Study 2 examined relationships between the IAS and mood, anxiety, psychopathology, neurodevelopmental traits, personality, and belief-related constructs, finding adaptive traits positively associated and maladaptive traits negatively associated with interoceptive scores. The 14-item version performed comparably to the original 21-item scale, with item-pairing enhancing interpretability; the Hungry-Thirsty and Bruise-Blood-sugar pairs showed the strongest associations. These findings support self-perceived interoceptive ability as a differentiated, system-specific construct.

articles.title: Self-Movement and Other-Movement Estimation Involve Distinct Multisensory Processing
articles.authors: Joshua David Haynes; Andrew P. Jones; Rebecca A. Champion; Boris Otkhmezuri; Graham Bell; Debbie Cane; Rosa Crunkhorn; Monty Silverdale; James Lilleker; Alan Carson
articles.abstract: Integration of multisensory information about self-movement is required both to estimate our own movement, but also to appropriately interpret the movement of other parts of the visual scene. Here we investigated whether the multisensory processes underlying these two tasks are the same or distinct. For a single group of participants, we assessed and compared multi-sensory integration performance in heading estimation and Scene-Relative Other-Movement (SROM) tasks. At the group level, integration was nearer to optimal (i.e. in line with Maximum Likelihood Estimation) in the heading task than the SROM task, though not all participants integrated optimally in either task. We found no evidence for correlation between integration performance across tasks, suggesting multi-sensory processing in the two tasks is distinct. We propose that these results reflect differences in the temporal dynamics of the two tasks and the neural pathways that might support this processing.

articles.title: Stress Beliefs Shape Daily Affective Reactivity to Social and Work Stressors: A 7-Day Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Johannes Andreas Christoph Laferton; Daniela Conrad; Frank Zimmermann-Viehoff; Stefanie Kunas; Frank Euteneuer; Susanne Fischer; Stefan Salzmann
articles.abstract: Stress beliefs—general expectations about the nature and consequences of stress—have been linked to health and performance, yet their role in shaping responses to everyday stress remains less understood. This study examined whether stress beliefs moderate affective reactivity and stress regulation strategies in response to naturally occurring stressors in daily life. In a 7-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study, 104 university students completed thrice-daily reports (1,939 observations) on social and work-related stressors, positive and negative affect, and two stress regulation strategies—situation selection and response modification—as proposed in the Stress Optimization Model (Crum, Jamieson, & Akinola, 2020). At baseline, stress beliefs were assessed alongside variables to characterize the sample. Negative stress beliefs moderated the association between daily stressors and positive affect: individuals with high negative stress beliefs showed reduced positive affect during social stress and no increase in positive affect under higher workload. In contrast, those with low or moderate negative stress beliefs maintained positive affect during social stress and showed increased positive affect under higher workload—consistent with a challenge-like appraisal. Additionally, controllability beliefs buffered increases in negative affect in response to daily social stress, with lower beliefs linked to stronger affective reactivity. In contrast, stress beliefs did not moderate associations between daily stressors and the investigated stress regulation strategies. These findings suggest that stress beliefs tune affective reactivity to everyday social and work stressors, identifying them as a potential intervention target given the established links between affect and long-term health. The generalizability of these findings should be confirmed across broader populations.

articles.title: Is it Reactive Aggression? Using Computational Methods to Explain Evolving Aggression
articles.authors: Fakhra Jabeen; Charlotte Gerritsen; Jan Treur
articles.abstract: Social media is one of the widely used channels for interpersonal communication, and to give personal feedback. However, negative feedback can affect the esteem and mental health of a person. This study presents a computational network model of a humanoid agent who gets (an) inappropriate feedback. It explains how he learns to react with his level of competence in this situation, although he dislikes the feedback. This model can help to detect and handle cyber-aggression and can be used as a building block to provide support to the victims.

articles.title: Item Features Affect How Well People Can Predict Self-Reported Personality Traces of Strangers
articles.authors: Richard Rau; Sebastian Kueppers; Mitja D Back; Michael P. Grosz
articles.abstract: Previous work suggests that self–other agreement in personality judgment is lower for evaluative than for neutral items. We tested whether this pattern generalizes to judgments collected with Who Knows, a mobile app in which users watch brief video clips of strangers and try to predict how targets answered highly concrete personality statements. The dataset comprised >340,000 predictions from >4,000 judges across 296 items and 75 targets. Contrary to prior findings, item evaluativeness did not reduce prediction accuracy with respect to targets’ self-reports. Instead, evaluativeness was positively associated with prediction accuracy for Likert-type items while no effect was observed for binary items. Other coded item features (e.g., base rate and psychological modality) showed no consistent associations with prediction accuracy across formats. We propose two boundary conditions that may help reconcile these results with earlier work: (a) the present item pool is unusually concrete, which alters the distribution and correlates of desirability/evaluativeness, and (b) judges were instructed to predict targets’ self-reports rather than provide their own impressions. Under this instruction, judges may partly rely on between-target differences in self-protective responding when forming predictions. These findings caution against transferring item-feature effects from adjective-based impression paradigms to concrete items and self-report prediction tasks.

articles.title: Predicting Effects of a Computational Empathetic Bot
articles.authors: Fakhra Jabeen
articles.abstract:
Chatbots or virtual agents are getting popular in many domains, for example, in academics, business, or healthcare sectors. They are tailored for specific scenarios, and current studies show that they help in reducing the workload of human experts. This study aims to present an architecture and design for a chatbot named as ‘Leo’. Leo is designed using psychological theories to provide support to people who are seeking emotional support. An experiment was conducted to evaluate the usability of Leo, in which 220 participants provided their feedback after having a conversation with Leo. The selected participants had anxiety and mood related issues reported in the past. Multiple Linear Regression was applied to predict the effects of chatbot towards Multiple Linear Regression was applied to predict the effects of chatbot towards supporting the users by regulating their mental
states. According to the results obtained from the Multiple Linear Regression, using left
a positive influence on the mood of the users, and they recommended Leo.

articles.title: Truth by repetition reliably differs between people over time
articles.authors: Jonas De keersmaecker; Brenton M. Wiernik; Arne Roets; Christian Unkelbach
articles.abstract: Repetition increases the believability of information. Despite the assumedly widespread (harmful) implications of this truth-by-repetition effect (TBRE), little is known about if and how repetition influences people differently. Across two longitudinal experiments (N1 = 113, Belgium; N2 = 430, UK), each consisting of five sessions over 33 days, we collected 108,600 truth judgments. Analyses showed that people differ in their TBRE across time, suggesting a trait-like disposition, which covaried with their Preference for Fluency. Notably, many participants showed stable TBREs that were small or close to zero, whereas relatively few showed large TBREs. We found no evidence for negative TBREs whereby repetition meaningfully decreases believability. The results highlight the value of multiple assessments and challenge the idea of a universal TBRE; repetition increases the believability of information – but not for everyone, and more so for some than others.

articles.title: Sequential Causal Decomposition for Reducing Social Disparities: A Step-by-Step Tutorial Using R
articles.authors: Su Yeon Kim; Soojin Park; Chioun Lee
articles.abstract: Persistent disparities in educational, economic, and health outcomes remain a central challenge for researchers and policymakers. There is a critical need to evaluate how these disparities would reduce if we intervened on specific, modifiable factors. Because social disparities are rarely the result of a single event, they must be analyzed as a sequence. This tutorial provides an accessible guide to implement Sequential Causal Decomposition Analysis in R. We walk applied researchers through the entire analytical steps: formulating research questions, drawing causal diagrams, assessing assumptions, selecting appropriate estimators. Then, we demonstrate implementing the analysis in R with a real-world example. The illustrated method offers users the flexibility to choose between the generalized linear model and machine learning approaches, both of which combined with a triply-robust estimator. As a result, both approaches provide a high-level protection to potential model misspecification. We illustrate this workflow with a simulated data based on the HSLS:09.

articles.title: Receptive Vocabulary Performance Varies with Depression
articles.authors: Michael J. Espero
articles.abstract:
Assessment of health and lifestyle factors in relation with receptive vocabulary across language groups is conducted as parameters are fixed and freed for estimation. Structural equation modeling (SEM) and multi-group structural equation modeling (MGSEM) is used to test the suitability of the model for reproducing the data sample
covariance matrix, the relationships of hypothesized constructs, and the tenability of equivalence across two participant samples. Most demonstrated acceptable global fit indices, however, following group isolated model fitting and re-fitting of MGSEMs (item-factor loadings, covariances, regression paths, and intercepts fixed and freed for estimation) - a parsimonious model predicting the strength of the influence of depression and alcohol experience equally between groups (fixed regression
parameters) on receptive vocabulary was chosen, reflecting structural invariance. The model suggests tenability of the observation of similarly negative impact of depression on receptive vocabulary performance regardless of participant group among included samples.

articles.title: Fixed versus Adaptive Word Lists: Effects on Spelling Outcomes in Adolescents
articles.authors: Dalia Martinez; Danielle Colenbrander; Signy Wegener; Tomohiro Inoue; George K. Georgiou; Anne Castles
articles.abstract: Adaptive word lists, which remove correctly spelled words from practice, may offer an efficient approach by reducing practice time. However, it remains unclear if these potential time-saving benefits may come at a learning cost relative to fixed word lists, in which all words receive equal practice regardless of performance. We examined the cost–benefit trade-off between these two approaches. A total of 113 Grade 7 and 8 students were randomly assigned to either the Adaptive List (AL; n = 58; 55.2% female; Mage= 12.4 years) or the Fixed List group (FL; n = 55; 50.9% female; Mage= 12.4 years) to complete three computer-based spelling practice sessions on 12 words with unpredictable spellings. The number of trials per session differed between conditions: in the AL group, correctly spelled words were dropped from further practice (12 to 36 trials per session); the FL group practiced each word three times per session over 36 trials. Students were assessed at pre-test, post-test, and two weeks later at follow-up on the spelling and reading of trained and untrained items. Results of generalized mixed-effects modeling revealed that practice sessions were significantly shorter for the AL group. However, the AL group showed reduced learning and more forgetting on spelling outcomes compared to the FL group. Differences between conditions did not emerge for reading. We discuss these findings in relation to item characteristics, distinctions between spelling and reading, and the advantages and limitations of each approach for classroom practice.

articles.title: Impossibility and Logical Contradictions Can Enhance the Perceived Value of Fictional Theological Propositions
articles.authors: Takuetsu Yajima; Eisuke Niida; Yo Nakawake
articles.abstract: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities. It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people’s evaluations of religious propositions. In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability. Those propositions were rated for impossibility and logical contradiction. A composite positive-evaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The result shows higher impossibility and higher logical contradiction predict higher positive evaluations of the propositions. These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

articles.title: A Neuroaffirmative Evidence Stack for Multi-Source Adult Neurodivergence Assessment: Framework Design and Formative Computational Evaluation
articles.authors: Lucas Fortaleza de Aquino Ferreira; Lenifer Siqueira Landim
articles.abstract: Background: Digital assessment of neurodivergent adults is hampered by a fundamental tension: self-report, informant-report, and performance measures often disagree, yet existing platforms typically collapse these discrepancies into a single score or discard them as noise. In autism and related neurodivergences, such disagreement can reflect clinically meaningful phenomena, including masking, context-dependent trait expression, informant-context mismatch, and limited insight, rather than invalid data. Current systems rarely make their integration logic auditable or neuroaffirmative. Objective: This methods paper presents the SPECTRA Evidence Stack, a formally specified three-layer framework (Response Quality, Multi-source Convergence, and Confidence Synthesis) designed to integrate heterogeneous assessment signals transparently. The framework produces structured outputs, including quality flags, convergence profiles, reason codes, and next-step recommendations, without claiming diagnostic validity. Methods: We describe the architecture, formal definitions, and rule logic of each layer. Response Quality flags identify data conditions requiring caution without pathologizing the respondent. Multi-source Convergence assigns interpretable discrepancy profiles across self-report, informant-report, and performance data. Confidence Synthesis combines these artifacts into an evidence-confidence band, mandatory reason codes, and recommended actions. We report a formative computational evaluation using a four-condition ablation design on 250 synthetic records, plus three clinical demonstration vignettes. Results: The full-stack condition produced higher and less variable confidence scores (mean 0.64, SD 0.09, 95% CI 0.63-0.65) than the no-convergence (mean 0.50, SD 0.12, 95% CI 0.48-0.51; paired Cohen dz=2.57) and baseline conditions (mean 0.50, SD 0.31, 95% CI 0.46-0.54). Discordance-sensitive cases showed the largest separation between full-stack and ablated conditions, demonstrating that the framework treats discrepancy as structured signal. Demonstration vignettes illustrated masking-compatible divergence, informant-context mismatch, and sparse-evidence scenarios. Conclusions: The SPECTRA Evidence Stack provides a replicable, auditable, and neuroaffirmative architecture for integrating multi-source neurodivergence assessment data. It makes uncertainty visible, preserves discrepancy as interpretable evidence, and supports shared clinical decision-making. This formative methods paper does not establish diagnostic accuracy; a subsequent clinical validation study against independent adjudication is planned.

articles.title: Who reciprocates whom? Mutual influence in emoticon use and perceived responsiveness between chat workers and young people seeking help
articles.authors: Gerard Chung; Andrew Zi Han Yee; Nataliya Thell; Lim Tse Min
articles.abstract:
Research on computer-mediated communication has shown that reciprocal emoticon and emoji
use predicts how warm, responsive, and engaging a text exchange is perceived to be. This work,
however, has been conducted almost entirely in symmetric dyads, such as peers, friends, dating
partners, or colleagues, in which both parties enter the exchange on equal terms. We extend this
literature to a role-asymmetric helping dyad, examining emoticon reciprocity between trained chat
workers and help-seeking young people in a Singapore youth chatline. Drawing on the Interpersonal
Process Model of Intimacy and Communication Accommodation Theory, we analysed 86,424 lagged
turns nested within 1,435 sessions using the Actor–Partner Interdependence Model, operationalising
emoticon use in both binary (presence) and count (intensity) forms. Three findings emerged. First,
emoticons were a routine feature of the channel (87% of sessions), with chat workers using more and a
narrower affirming repertoire than users. Second, positive actor and partner effects were present in
both directions, but the partner effect from chat worker to user was substantially larger than the
reverse, indicating asymmetric reciprocity tracking the role and power asymmetry of the dyad. Third,
partner effects were stronger in sessions rated higher on worker responsiveness and session
satisfaction; actor effects were also moderated by both ratings, though in opposing directions
depending on operationalisation. What matters in text-based help, our results suggest, is not either
party's emoticon use considered alone but the reciprocal exchange between them.

articles.title: Investigating the Origins of Partisanship: What Motivates Children to Preferentially Endorse Their Ingroups’ Claims?
articles.authors: Bethany Lassetter; Natalie Ann Hutchins; Lucas P Butler; Andrei Cimpian
articles.abstract: Adults often endorse empirical claims along partisan lines, sometimes agreeing with their ingroup even when the evidence suggests otherwise. A developmental approach can clarify the motives underlying this phenomenon by examining it early, before political identities are entrenched. We tested two possible motives underlying children’s partisan endorsement: Do children endorse their ingroup’s empirical claims because they believe the ingroup is a reliable guide to truth (an epistemic motive), or because public agreement signals loyalty and strengthens group bonds (an affiliative motive)? Study 1 (N = 98; ages 5–7) replicated the basic partisanship phenomenon in childhood: Children assigned to a minimal group endorsed their ingroup’s claims more often than children in a no-group control condition, establishing that group membership provides a partisan “boost” beyond what perceptual evidence alone would warrant. Studies 2 and 3 then probed motives in complementary ways: Study 2 (N = 208; ages 6–9) removed the social-audience benefits of endorsing the ingroup by having children respond privately, whereas Study 3 (N = 172; ages 6–9) increased the value of accuracy by incentivizing correct judgments. Partisan endorsement was absent under private responding and significantly reduced by accuracy incentives. Overall, the pattern across studies was more consistent with an affiliative motive than an epistemic one: Children’s partisan endorsement appears to function as public signaling of group support rather than solely as a reflection of epistemic trust in the ingroup. These findings speak to the developmental origins of partisan cognition and potential levers for encouraging evidence-based reasoning.

articles.title: Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM) in a 16-Year-Old Male: Investigating Involuntary Autobiographical Memory With Questionnaire and Laboratory Methods
articles.authors: Krystian Barzykowski; Valerio Santangelo; Lia Kvavilashvili; Chris Moulin
articles.abstract:
Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM) is characterized by an exceptional ability
to recall personal past events with remarkable accuracy and detail. While the mechanisms
underlying this ability have begun to be elucidated, research so far has largely focused mainly
on voluntary retrieval processes. The present study aimed to investigate autobiographical
memory functioning in a single HSAM case (KCL), with a particular focus on involuntary
autobiographical memories (IAMs). We combined standardized HSAM screening procedures
with a multi-method assessment of autobiographical memory. General autobiographical
functioning was assessed using the Autobiographical Recollection Test (ART) and the Survey
of Autobiographical Memory (SAM). Additional measures captured general memory
functioning, mind-wandering, metacognitive and phenomenological characteristics, cognitive
control, and affective and personality variables. IAMs were assessed using both self-report
(Involuntary Autobiographical Memory Inventory; IAMI) and a laboratory vigilance task with
incidental cue-words and probe-caught thought sampling. KCL met established HSAM criteria
and exhibited a markedly elevated frequency of IAMs relative to a comparison group, both in
self-report and laboratory measures. Crucially, this increase did not reflect a general rise in
spontaneous cognition, as overall task-unrelated thought frequency remained comparable, but
rather a selective bias toward autobiographical content. At the same time, KCL did not differ
from the general population in overall phenomenological experience of remembering, although
he reported elevated autobiographical memory ability alongside increased confidence in
memory accuracy. The results highlight the central role of involuntary remembering and point
to altered cue sensitivity and lowered retrieval thresholds as key mechanisms underlying
exceptional autobiographical memory.

articles.title: Format-invariant semantic dimensions structure food similarity judgments
articles.authors: Jason Avery; Charles Zheng; Caroline Candy; Andrew Persichetti; Alex Martin
articles.abstract: Our knowledge about food integrates sensory, affective, functional, and cultural information that is not reducible to visual appearance or nutritional composition. We asked whether human food similarity judgments are organized by semantic dimensions that generalize across presentation format. Participants completed large-scale odd-one-out triplet tasks for the same 68 foods presented either as photographs or written names, fully sampling all possible triplets in each modality. We fit VICE, a sparse Bayesian embedding model, independently to image and word judgments, then identified stable dimensions matched across modalities. This procedure revealed nine format-invariant consensus dimensions. These consensus dimensions accounted for nearly all predictable triplet behavior, outperforming models based on explicit food property ratings, objective macronutrients, low-level image statistics, and general object-property embeddings. The dimensions showed interpretable relationships with subjective food properties and, to a lesser extent, nutritional content, and showed partial overlap with the broader THINGS object-property space. Out-of-sample validation showed that the same dimensions generalized to independent food similarity datasets. Finally, analyses of dimension contributions across triplet judgments indicated that food similarity is not well described as a strictly two-dimensional space or a simple hierarchy. Instead, a small number of broad dimensions that capture coarse distinctions among food types coexist with finer-grained dimensions that discriminate both within and across those divisions. These findings suggest that food knowledge is organized by a multidimensional semantic structure that is stable across format, partly shared with general object cognition, and enriched by food-specific distinctions.

articles.title: On the Psychophysics of Morality: Moral choices obey Weber’s law
articles.authors: Ansgar D Endress; Peter Ayton
articles.abstract: Moral decisions are often cast as a conflict between utilitarianism (maximizing good) and deontology (following rules). We propose a unitary psychophysical model where moral decisions operate like other perceptual systems and track the subjective (information-theoretic) certainty that outcomes achieve the greater good. Due to psychophysical noise, decisions are governed by Weber’s law, with utilitarian and deontological responses as high- vs. low-uncertainty limit cases. Participants rated the acceptability of sacrificing fewer ‘victims’ to save more ‘beneficiaries.’ Consistent with this model, acceptability tracked the ratio of beneficiaries to victims (beneficiary:victim Weber ratios), but not utility (net survivors) or harm (victims). With decreased uncertainty (using decisions concerning eco- nomic goods that had clearer values than human lives), responses became more ‘utilitarian’; with increased attention to victims (via emotional manipulations), responses became more ‘deontological’, but always tracked the beneficiary:victim Weber ratios. Frontier large language models from three different jurisdictions (though not smaller models) partially reproduced human behavior, but used qualitatively different heuristics from humans and generally prioritized harm or utility over beneficiary:victim ratios. Beyond moral decision making, the same model provides the first mechanistic and parameter-free explanation of loss-aversion. People, but not machines, thus seek the greater good, but do so under perceptual noise.

articles.title: The interplay between daily loneliness and psychopathology in a heterogeneous clinical sample: A multilevel network analysis
articles.authors: Daniel Dančík; Adam Kurilla; Radoslav Lošonský; Alica Hujsová; Natália Čavojská; Sebastián Petreje; Julia; Valentína Cviková; Sára Majsniarová; Petra Brandoburová
articles.abstract: Loneliness is increasingly conceptualized as a dynamic, transdiagnostic phenomenon, yet its short-term links with psychopathology remain unclear. Eighty-four psychiatric patients completed experience sampling assessments three times daily for 30 days. Multilevel vector autoregressive models estimated temporal, contemporaneous, and between-subject networks of loneliness and eight psychopathological domains. Loneliness showed substantial within-subject variability and autoregressive persistence. It was associated with attachment insecurity across all network levels, with reciprocal temporal associations between the two constructs. Higher loneliness predicted lower subsequent positive affect, while contemporaneously it was associated with attachment insecurity, greater negative affect, and lower positive affect. Attachment insecurity was linked to interpersonal difficulties, including suspiciousness, distrust, and conflicts, across all network levels, and to negative affect temporally and contemporaneously. Overall, loneliness emerged as a dynamic, yet persistent socio-emotional experience embedded within affective and interpersonal processes characterized by attachment insecurity and heightened sensitivity to interpersonal threat. These processes warrant experimental and intervention-based investigation.

articles.title: Does Visual Privacy Leakage Compromise Fairness in Multimodal Automated Feedback? Extending Group Fairness to Privacy Contexts
articles.authors: Hai Li; Wanli Xing; Chenglu Li; Neil Thomas Heffernan
articles.abstract:
Multimodal automated feedback systems are core components of next-generation K--12 mathematics learning interfaces, processing textual responses and handwritten images for large-scale personalized learning. When students upload assignment images in uncontrolled environments, visual privacy information such as faces and hands may be inadvertently captured, potentially correlating with contextual factors including the photo-taking environment, image quality, student effort, assignment type, and device access, thereby raising critical algorithmic fairness concerns in high-stakes educational assessment.

This study extends group fairness from traditional demographic attributes to privacy contexts by treating privacy leakage status and type as group-defining characteristics. We propose a component-driven multimodal feedback model that simulates teachers' cognitive processes through four components: Mathematical Element Masking (MEM), Cross-Modal Consistency Verification (CMCV), Question--Answer Interaction (QAI), and Scoring Prototype Contrastive Learning (SPCL). The optimal configuration, MatCha with all components, achieves an MSE of 0.0906 and an \(R^2\) of 0.1686, representing a 257.2\% improvement in explanatory power over the baseline. This performance is highly competitive given the inherent subjectivity of open-ended mathematical scoring.

Using a dual-perspective fairness framework that distinguishes model fairness (opportunity allocation) from error fairness (service quality), we identify a privacy leakage paradox: samples containing privacy leakage exhibit superior predictive accuracy yet systematically lower high-score opportunity rates. The overall disparate impact ratio for privacy leakage is 0.7565, falling below the legal threshold of 0.80, while the ratio for facial leakage is 0.8274, approaching the fairness boundary. No substantial gender bias is detected under facial leakage conditions.

articles.title: Shaping New Perceptions: A Preliminary Multi-Method Investigation of Changes in Hostile Attributions following a Psychoeducational Mentalization-Based Treatment Module
articles.authors: Marta Bodecka-Zych; Dorota Jasielska; Monika Olga Jańczak; Joanna Rajchert; Jean Gagnon; Anna Zajenkowska
articles.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Mentalization-Based Treatment (MBT), including brief psychoeducational modules, has shown promising effects in reducing aggression among adolescents and forensic populations. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which MBT exerts its effects. This preliminary pilot study aimed to explore changes in hostile attribution following participation in an MBT psychoeducational module using a multimodal assessment approach.
Methods: The six sessions (three meetings) of the MBT-Introductory Group were delivered to a total of 58 participants across four groups: inmates, juvenile delinquents, high school students, and young adults. Pre- and post-intervention assessments combined quantitative measures with qualitative analyses to examine changes in different facets of hostile attribution. Tasks included ambiguous facial expression recognition, interpretation of visual scenes, the Ambiguous Intentions and Hostility Questionnaire, and interpretation of self-recalled interpersonal situations.
Results: Participation in the MBT module was associated with a reduction in hostile attributions among young adults and juvenile offenders; results among high school students were mixed depending on the task type, while among inmates, changes were observed only for specific stimulus formats.
Conclusions: Despite several limitations, this preliminary study suggests that psychoeducational MBT modules may be associated with changes in hostile attribution bias. The findings suggest that mentalization-based frameworks may represent a potentially promising direction for preventive and rehabilitative interventions for at-risk youth, including brief psychoeducational formats.
Keywords: hostile attributions, mentalization-based treatment, inmates, juvenile delinquents

articles.title: Who gets to be their true selves at work?
articles.authors: Jordan Wylie; Erica R. Bailey; Ana Gantman
articles.abstract: People spend a lot of time at work, and increasingly look to their careers as a place to express their true, authentic selves. We examine two career pathways to the true self at work: moral careers (e.g., those in healthcare, social work), which should foster authenticity because morality is central to identity and the true self, and aesthetic careers (e.g., those in artistic and creative fields), which should foster authenticity through the freedom and autonomy they afford. Across three experiments (N = 1,232) and one archival study using the General Social Survey (GSS; N = 72,390), we compare these pathways from both third- and first-person perspectives. Study 1 shows that job seekers value the freedom and autonomy we theorize aesthetic careers provide. Study 2 shows that third-party observers expect aesthetic careers to afford greater freedom, access to the true self, happiness, and life satisfaction than moral careers. Study 3 uses the GSS and reveals the opposite pattern: people in moral careers report greater happiness and job satisfaction than those in aesthetic or control careers. Study 4 reconciles this discrepancy by directly comparing third- and first-person judgments about the true self. We find that expectations about aesthetic careers largely match reality, but that observers systematically underestimate the psychological benefits of moral careers. Together, these findings suggest that aesthetic careers offer a path to the true self and happiness at work, while the comparable, and sometimes greater, benefits of moral careers go underappreciated.

articles.title: Hard bargains and even splits: Fairness judgments track bargaining power across diverse cultures
articles.authors: Arthur Le Pargneux; Xavier Roberts-Gaal; Lucas Woodley; Joshua D. Greene; Fiery Andrews Cushman
articles.abstract:
What is the fair way to distribute resources? Past research highlights egalitarian and redistributive intuitions that favor the disadvantaged. Contractualist theories propose moral judgments mirror what rational agents would agree to, favoring parties in advantaged bargaining positions. We reconcile these views, showing people think it fair to favor the advantaged when they have more bargaining power, but to favor the disadvantaged in a non-bargaining context. Specifically, across nine countries, participants (n = 6,304) make third-party judgments about the
morally best split of a fixed amount. When the split requires agreement (bilateral negotiation in Study 1; third-party negotiation in Study 2), moral judgments overwhelmingly track bargaining power and can be predicted with striking quantitative precision. When the split is determined by
a unilateral donation and existing inequalities do not alter bargaining positions, moral intuitions
are reversed, reflecting redistributive or egalitarian concerns.

articles.title: TuneTwins: An Intrinsically Motivating Game Paradigm for Scalable Music Cognition Research
articles.authors: Jiaxin Li; David John Baker; John Ashley Burgoyne; Henkjan Honing
articles.abstract: Researchers across the behavioral sciences are increasingly using games as a means of data collection. Intrinsically motivating digital games are especially promising for music cognition, where large, diverse, and engaged samples are needed. In this article, we focus on a specific class of game paradigms suited to cross-cultural contexts and applicable across the developmental lifespan: auditory matching-pairs (Memory) games. We present the conception, design, and initial evaluation of TuneTwins, a solitaire auditory matching-pairs paradigm developed to study musical memory and auditory cognition. Building on self-determination theory and prior game-based research, TuneTwins employs an 8-pair (4 × 4) board to balance playability with psychometric sensitivity. Our web-based auditory adaptation introduces clear visual–auditory mappings, a three-click turn structure, and a dual scoring system that distinguishes memorized matches from lucky guesses and memory errors. Large-scale simulations of chance and optimal strategies guided the choice of board size, demonstrating that this configuration yields meaningful separation between performance extremes while avoiding ceiling effects. We further report empirical evidence from three implementations: a proof-of-concept online study, a cross-cultural field study with Mbendjele BaYaka hunter-gatherers, and an online global deployment. Across these settings, TuneTwins captured systematic performance differences between stimulus conditions and elicited high voluntary engagement, including repeated play and the completion of multiple difficulty levels. We argue that matching-pairs games such as TuneTwins provide an engaging, intuitive, and scalable paradigm for collecting behavioral data using primarily auditory stimuli—and that they can be used to probe the mental representation of music across cultures, across development, and potentially across species.

articles.title: The effects of introducing measurement-based care in outpatient psychotherapy: a naturalistic study
articles.authors: Tim Kaiser; Selin Demir; Eva-Lotta Brakemeier
articles.abstract:
Objective. This study investigated the effectiveness of a newly implemented routine outcome monitoring and feedback system, the Greifswald Psychotherapy Navigation System (GPNS). 
Methods. 261 patients (M_age = 33 years, 79% female) completed individual cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) from 61 psychotherapists. Using Bayesian instrumental variable estimation, we estimated the local average treatment effect (LATE) of using the GPNS on post-treatment symptom severity and personality impairment. Sensitivity analyses were performed to estimate the robustness of our estimates.
Results. Using the GPNS significantly reduced post-treatment symptom severity (LATE = -0.11, 95% CrI: -0.18; -0.03) and personality impairment (LATE = -2.65, 95% CrI: -3.72; -1.58). Sensitivity analyses showed that the effects were robust to plausible residual confounding. 
Conclusion. The GPNS shows promise for improving outcomes of CBT. Future prospective trials should be conducted to obtain a more generalizable estimate of its effect.

articles.title: Economic Growth and Emotional Well-Being: Longitudinal Evidence from 33 European Countries
articles.authors: Filip Fors Connolly; Mikael Hjerm; Tommy Gärling
articles.abstract: The relationship between economic growth and emotional well-being remains poorly understood relative to life satisfaction, largely due to methodological limitations. Using psychometrically robust measures we examined how national income relates to emotional well-being. Analyzing 178,948 participants across 33 European countries in four European Social Survey waves (2006, 2012, 2014, 2023), we constructed a reliable emotional well-being measure and compared it with single-item life satisfaction. Both showed strong positive cross-sectional correlations with GDP per capita. Linear mixed-effects models revealed economic growth significantly predicts within-country increases in both emotional well-being and life satisfaction. These findings demonstrate that economic development improves both cognitive and affective dimensions of subjective well-being, contradicting previous research suggesting a weak association with emotional experiences. Economic growth thus remains important for improving citizens' daily emotional experiences, not merely their life evaluations, highlighting the continued relevance of economic development for well-being.

articles.title: Factors Associated with Students’ Perceived Competence Using Statistical Software
articles.authors: Alyssa Counsell
articles.abstract: Statistical software is used in many statistics courses across a wide range of disciplines. However, minimal research examines how students’ attitudes and experience relate to feeling competent using statistical software by the end of a statistics course. In this study, I examined variables relevant from two competing theories (expectancy-value theory; EVT, and technology acceptance model; TAM) to examine which ones were most strongly associated with students’ perceived competence using statistical software by the end of a statistics course. Participants came from two samples; sample 1 included undergraduate students learning a point-click software in the social sciences (n =110); sample 2 included students learning R in a Masters program in analytics (n = 193). In both samples, the TAM-aligned variables had higher correlations with perceived competence than the EVT-aligned statistics attitudes variables. However, the correlations of EVT-aligned variables tended to be stronger in sample 2. Analysis of open-ended data asking about factors impacting software competence resulted in somewhat different findings across the samples. Sample 1 participants were more likely to focus on course-specific resources such as course manuals or instructor impacts, whereas sample 2 participants were more likely to focus on the importance of real-world applications, previous experience, and intrinsic factors.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence Systems Distort Upstream Selection in Human Social Learning
articles.authors: William J. Brady; Chen-Wei Yu; Nicholas Ornstein; Bolun Sun; Joshua Conrad Jackson
articles.abstract: Humans are social learners who depend on observing others to acquire knowledge, norms, and behaviors, a capacity that underlies cumulative cultural evolution. Social learning unfolds in two stages: upstream selection determines what information becomes visible, and downstream selection determines what learners copy from that visible sample. Downstream selection occurs through biases such as conformity bias (copying what appears common) and prestige bias (copying those who appear highly respected). These downstream biases can be adaptive when upstream selection yields a sample that reflects the population's true distribution, so that what appears common is actually common and those who appear respected are actually competent. We argue that digital technologies disrupt this condition, creating an upstream selection problem. Engagement-based algorithms amplify the tails of the distribution, surfacing rare and extreme content, whereas generative AI collapses it toward the mode, erasing the surrounding diversity. Crucially, in each system the optimization signal shapes both visibility and prestige. For engagement-based algorithms, the signal is engagement: creators who post extreme content become more visible and, through the likes, shares, and followers, appear more prestigious. For generative AI, the signal is statistical typicality: it makes the modal answer dominant and, with no alternatives shown, makes the model that produced it appear more prestigious. These distortions can give rise to emergent group-level phenomena, including pluralistic ignorance and false consensus. Synthesizing evidence across psychology, cultural evolution, and computational social science, we provide a framework for how digital technologies disrupt social learning and outline interventions for restoring functional cultural transmission.

articles.title: Delusions are Related to Aberrant Causal Generalization
articles.authors: Martin Meyer; Santiago Castiello; Samuel Paskewitz; Philip R. Corlett
articles.abstract: Generalization tendencies might simultaneously explain the emergence and maintenance of delusional beliefs. On the one hand, people with a tendency to under-generalize information might produce “overfit” explanatory models and accordingly fail to recognize when new data bears on them; on the other hand, people with a tendency to over-generalize information might produce “underfit” explanatory models and accordingly update them in inappropriate scenarios. To adjudicate between these hypotheses, we test whether delusions predict performance on a classic stimulus generalization paradigm (the peak shift). The behavioral data indicate that higher delusionality predicts over-generalization of learned causal relationships and under-generalization of learned absence of causality. Computational modeling largely reveals the driving mechanism to be stochasticity (and perhaps prediction error), however, specific aspects of delusionality (distress, contents) relate to different generalization tendencies.

articles.title: The Effects of a Yoga Intervention on Adults with Intellectual Disabilities (ID). A systematic review.
articles.authors: Louise Gates
articles.abstract:
Background: Adults with ID are significantly more likely to be overweight or obese, and they are more likely to suffer from mental illness such as anxiety or depression. Currently, there is limited research into non-pharmacological approaches to enhancing wellbeing for adults with ID. Various studies have examined the positive impact of yoga interventions on the general population. However, to date, few studies have looked into psychosocial interventions (such as yoga) for adults with ID.
Methods: The following databases were searched: Cochrane, SCOPUS, Medline, AMED, CINHAL, SportsDiscus, PsychARTICLES and PsychINFO. The inclusion and exclusion criteria were independently applied by one researcher. A second reviewer then checked the individual papers against these criteria. Data was then extracted from the studies selected for inclusion in the review.
Results: One study was included in this review. This was the only study deemed eligible for inclusion when the inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied. The paper was rated as having a medium risk of bias.
Conclusion: There is an extremely limited amount of published research available on the effects of yoga on adults with ID. This review concludes that – to support any initial positive findings on the implementation of yoga as an activity for this population group – more extensive, higher quality, and larger scale research is needed.

articles.title: What is the Feasibility and Benefit of Psychosocial Interventions for Adults with Intellectual Disabilities and Associated Mental Health Conditions? A systematic review.
articles.authors: Louise Gates
articles.abstract:
Background: Mental illness is highly prevalent amongst people with ID, and those affected are treated with often complex and sometimes numerous pharmacological treatments. It is clear that high-quality studies are needed to assess the feasibility of implementation of psychosocial interventions as alternative or adjunct treatments.
Methods: One reviewer independently applied the inclusion criteria to the search results and extracted data from the selected studies for inclusion in the review. All papers for inclusion were reviewed by a second reviewer, as were the reasons for excluding other papers. The databases searched were Cochrane, SCOPUS, Medline, AMED, CINHAL, SportsDiscus, PsychARTICLES, and PsychINFO.
Results: Four studies were included in this review. These were the only studies deemed eligible for inclusion and all were rated as having a low risk of bias.
Conclusion: There is a dearth of literature on psychosocial interventions for adults with ID and associated mental health conditions. This review provides evidence that more studies should be undertaken to assess the feasibility and implementation of psychosocial interventions with this vulnerable population group.

articles.title: What is the Feasibility and Scientific Benefit of Laughter Yoga Vs Vinyasa Yoga as a Psychosocial Intervention for Adults Experiencing Depression and Anxiety Secondary to Learning Disability?
articles.authors: Louise Gates; Martin Bollard; Derek Renshaw
articles.abstract:
Background: This feasibility study explored the potential of laughter yoga (LY) compared with vinyasa yoga (VY), as a psychosocial intervention for adults with learning disabilities (LD) experiencing depression and anxiety. No studies have previously investigated the effects of yoga on anxiety and depression in adults with intellectual disabilities, making this the first to assess two yoga styles in this context.
Methods: Thirteen participants were randomly assigned to LY (n=4), vinyasa yoga (VY; n=4), or a control group (n=5). Quantitative measures included mood rating scales, blood pressure, and salivary cortisol, assessed at baseline, week 3, week 6, and week 10. Qualitative data were collected through interviews. LY was found to be feasible and well-received. Results: While no significant effects were observed for depression, blood pressure, or cortisol, anxiety levels showed a significant reduction over time (F (3, 24) = 4.369; p = .014). Thematic analysis revealed five key themes, with two focusing on positive participant feedback and emotional well-being. 
Conclusion: The study demonstrates the acceptability of LY and suggests its potential as a non-pharmacological intervention for mental health in adults with LD. These findings support the need for a full-scale randomized controlled trial to further evaluate LY’s efficacy. This research contributes to the limited evidence base on yoga interventions for adults with LD (Chong et al., 2011; Kataria, 2002; Rao et al., 2013) and highlights the importance of inclusive, adaptable approaches to mental health support.
Keywords: yoga, laughter yoga, vinyasa yoga, anxiety, depression, learning disability, adults

articles.title: Stories for change: A theory informed, co produced method for developing lived experience narratives for behaviour change interventions
articles.authors: Emma Davies; Jennifer Seddon; Abi Rose; Cat Butler; Anne Greaves; Eila Watson; Fiona Matley
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Storytelling is increasingly used in health behaviour change interventions, but there is limited guidance on how to develop stories that are not only engaging and acceptable, but also theoretically robust and capable of functioning as active intervention components. This paper aimed to describe and reflect on a theory-informed, co-produced method for developing lived-experience narratives for behaviour change interventions.
Design: Qualitative interviews, co-production, and acceptability testing within the development of the SPACES intervention for alcohol reduction in mid-life women.
Methods: Lived-experience narratives were generated through 21 biographic-narrative interviews with mid-life women who were considering reducing their drinking or had recently done so. Transcripts were analysed using a structured story-component extraction proforma capturing Character, Context, Motives, Helpers, and Resolution. Extracted material was mapped to COM-B domains, behaviour change techniques, and mechanisms of action, aligned with the intervention logic model, and developed into intervention-ready stories. Stories were further refined through co-production with a public advisory group and acceptability testing with 28 target users.
Results: The method provided a structured way to develop authentic stories while embedding behaviour change content. Preliminary acceptability work suggested that stories were experienced as relatable, supportive, and non-judgemental, and that co-production and feedback were central to refining realism, clarity, and relevance.
Conclusions: Hypothesised mechanisms and efficacy of SPACES remain to be tested. This paper provides practical methodological guidance for developing theory-informed, co-produced stories as components of behaviour change interventions.

articles.title: The risks of conflating anhedonia with apathy
articles.authors: Sijia Zhao; Mercè Correa; John Salamone; Masud Husain
articles.abstract: The capacity for pleasure is distinct from the desire for reward, or the effort required to obtain it. Yet a persistent trend in translational research conflates these dissociable processes, by absorbing motivational dysfunctions such as anergia/fatigue, avolition, and clinical apathy—involving a significant reduction in goal-directed behaviour—into the definition of anhedonia. This is not simply a semantic issue. By collapsing separable aspects of motivation into a single hedonic label, the field risks misdirecting therapeutic development; treatments targeting pleasure may be ineffective for patients whose primary deficit is in behavioural activation. In this Perspective, we propose deconstructing the reward-pursuit cycle into three mechanistically distinct stages — liking, wanting, and acting to fulfil goals—and show that much of what is labelled ‘anhedonia’ in translational models instead reflects impaired behavioural activation, a core feature of clinical apathy. Restoring this distinction is essential for precision phenotyping and mechanism-based treatment development.

articles.title: Cuing the future to reduce delay discounting: EEG correlates of value and vividness
articles.authors: Isaac Kinley; Jana Lau; Donna Rose Addis
articles.abstract: The tendency to discount future reward can be reduced when individuals are cued to imagine future events. This "cue effect" has been studied using fMRI, but the current work is the first to investigate it using EEG. We found that more subjectively vivid imagination of the future encouraged more farsighted decisions, and that subjective vividness was higher when larger delayed rewards were available. Using time-frequency partial least squares analysis, we identified a pattern of enhanced gamma and reduced theta power that correlated with the subjective value of delayed rewards on trials without cues. We also found a pattern of reduced parietal alpha power that was associated with subjective vividness on trials with cues. We contextualize these findings within the broader EEG literature on reward valuation, mental event simulation, and mental imagery.

articles.title: Non-conscious knowledge of complex regularities supports instrumental conditioning: A registered report
articles.authors: Răzvan Jurchiș; Andrei Preda; Andrei Razvan Costea; Lina Skora
articles.abstract: Instrumental conditioning (IC) consists in actively learning to approach rewarding stimuli and to avoid punishing stimuli. This central process for adaptation requires a relatively high computational capacity because it entails the integration of knowledge regarding stimuli, behaviours, and outcomes. Recent studies using subliminal exposure show that IC occurs only for consciously perceived stimuli, suggesting that IC may require awareness. In the present study, we investigated whether IC could occur when implicit processing is stimulated not by subliminal exposure but by employing predictive regularities that are complex and difficult to detect consciously. In a novel IC task based on the artificial grammar learning task, participants gave approach (Go) or avoidance responses (No-Go) to strings from two grammars. Unbeknown to them, one of the grammars was reward-predictive and the other was punishment-predictive. Trial-by-trial measures assessed participants’ awareness of the grammar structures and of their judgments regarding the predictive value of the strings. In both an IC phase and a delayed responding phase, we found that participants responded adaptively when they were aware of the regularities and, also, when they were not. Importantly, we found reliable evidence that non-conscious regularities produced adaptive responding only when they produced conscious judgments regarding the predictive values of the stimuli. When judgment knowledge was unconscious, data were insensitive or more consistent with chance performance. This suggests that IC may be produced by a combination of unconscious learning and conscious integration.

articles.title: Speech activity confounds respiratory sinus arrhythmia reactivity in psychophysiological research: how to detect and control for the effects of speech in daily life
articles.authors: Melisa Saygin; Martin Gevonden; Eco de Geus
articles.abstract: Speaking is a recurring activity that interferes with the measurement of the physiological stress response. Unique respiratory demands of speech amplify respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) when cardiac vagal activity may be unchanged or withdrawn. While this confounding may be experimentally controlled in laboratory settings, a speech activity detection model or, alternatively, an RSA metric that controls for the respiratory demands of speech is needed in daily life research. Here, we first validate an accelerometer-based speech detection model and impedance pneumography-based respiration assessment in naturalistic settings, using a throat microphone and respiratory inductance pneumography (RIP) as respective ground truths. Across participants, the accelerometer-based speech detection model showed good concurrent and criterion validity (71.6% sensitivity, 83.9% specificity, 84.4% AUC, .43 Matthews correlation coefficient). Impedance-based respiratory parameters showed good-to-moderate concurrent and criterion validity for breathing period (.59 ≤ r ≤ .71) and tidal volume (.50 ≤ r ≤ .54) but weak validity for inspiration-to-expiration duration (IE)-ratio (.27 ≤ r ≤ .43). Next, using mixed models, we confirmed that speech significantly shortens interbeat interval (by 75.2 ms) while it, counterintuitively, inflates RSA (by 25.3 ms) within individuals. After normalization by tidal volume, RSA showed the expected decrease in response to speech in sitting postures, but it required further control for inspiration-to-expiration duration (IE)-ratio in standing posture.
