Examination of individual participant slopes revealed IE-ratio controlled tidal volume-normalized RSA successfully eliminated the speech-related inflation of RSA for all participants. We recommend reporting IE-controlled tidal volume-normalized RSA in protocols involving speech, whether based on laboratory or ambulatory data. As speech also impacts a host of autonomic nervous system-related parameters other than RSA, the validated speech activity detection model can have wider utility to help disentangle psychophysiological reactivity.

articles.title: Twin Analyses Without Zygosity Information: The Promise and Pitfalls of the Normal Finite-Mixture-Distribution Twin Model
articles.authors: Madelief Isabel Kuijper; Camiel M. van der Laan; Abe Dirk Hofman; Elsje van Bergen; Bruno Sauce
articles.abstract: Twin designs offer a powerful framework for disentangling genetic and environmental sources of individual differences, but require zygosity information that is often unavailable. When zygosity is unknown, analyses may still be possible using a normal finite-mixture-distribution model. This model assumes that the bivariate twin phenotype is normally distributed within each zygosity group, an assumption that cannot be directly verified because zygosity is unobserved. We conducted a simulation study to determine how well the normal finite-mixture-distribution model recovered parameters if this assumption is violated and if the twin difference distribution could serve as a diagnostic for violations. In univariate and bivariate simulations, we varied sample size, variance structure and the degree and source of kurtosis. We examined whether marginal score transformations reduce bias. We applied univariate and bivariate models to educational gaming data with unknown zygosity. Simulation estimates were most precise at high heritability and remained reasonably stable with samples as small as 200 pairs. Excess kurtosis in twin difference scores substantially biased estimates, and marginal transformations did not meaningfully reduce bias. Kurtosis-related bias was smaller in the bivariate model than in the univariate model. Empirical estimates based on the univariate model seemed highly biased, producing very high heritability estimates (0.91–0.99), except for the measure of division-skills (A = 0.58, C= 0, E= 0.42). Estimates based on the bivariate model seemed less biased, but unstable. Although mixture modelling may be used for twin-analyses without zygosity information, violations of bivariate normality may introduce considerable, difficult-to-detect bias, warranting careful interpretation of results.

articles.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depression: A within-network resting state functional connectivity study
articles.authors: Nora de Bode; Emese Kroon; Jia Hua Hsieh; Francesca Filbey; Janna Cousijn
articles.abstract:
Background: Cannabis Use Disorder (CUD) and comorbid depressive symptoms are a prevalent mental health concern. However, knowledge about potentially shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remains mixed. Therefore, this study systematically investigated the role of depressive symptoms in the relationship between CUD, cannabis use characteristics, and within-network resting state functional connectivity (RSFC) in multiple networks implicated in both CUD and depression: the Executive Control Network (ECN), the Salience Network (SN), the Default Mode Network (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia Network (BGN).
Methods: In 152 participants with CUD and 114 controls, we examined the effects of group (CUD versus control), depressive symptoms, and their interaction on within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we further assessed the effects of depression diagnosis, cannabis use characteristics, and their interaction with depressive symptoms on within-network RSFC. We also tested associations between behavioral measures of depression and cannabis use. Bayesian analyses quantified the strength of all evidence.
Results: Although symptoms of depression were associated with CUD severity, there were no direct effects of depressive symptoms, nor any interaction effects between depressive symptoms, CUD status, or other cannabis use characteristics on within-network RSFC. In most networks, exploratory Bayesian analyses provided moderate to strong evidence in favor of the null hypotheses. 
Conclusion: The absence of significant group differences in within-network RSFC suggests it is not a robust marker in samples characterized by having a CUD and comorbid depressive symptoms, compared to controls. Instead, potentially individual characteristics, such as greater depression severity and heaviness of use, may contribute to altered RSFC.

articles.title: Purpose in life and markers of affective, behavioral, cognitive, and relational engagement measured across moments in daily life
articles.authors: Angelina Sutin; Martina Luchetti; Antonio Terracciano
articles.abstract: Engagement is a key factor in models of both purpose in life and cognitive health. These models usually measure engagement as participation in specific activities, whereas models of education and employment operationalize engagement as having specific affective, behavioral, cognitive, and relational components. As a step toward a more comprehensive model of purpose and cognitive health in middle and older adulthood, this research examines the association between dispositional purpose and metrics of these components of engagement reported across moments in daily life using ecological momentary assessment methodology. Participants (N=2577; Mage=63.52; SD=11.24) reported on their momentary engagement three times a day for eight days (>48,000 momentary assessments; 79% compliance). Higher dispositional purpose in life was associated with greater affective (e.g., positive affect; b=11.49 [SE=.61]), behavioral (e.g., persistent; b=10.20 [SE=.48]), cognitive (e.g., attentive; b=8.99 [SE=.46]), and relational (e.g., feeling connected; b=7.98 [SE=.57]) engagement in daily life (ps<.001). These associations were not moderated by sociodemographic factors. Higher purpose was mostly unrelated to variability in these metrics accounting for mean engagement: Participants higher in purpose had less variability because their average engagement was high. Greater engagement may be a mechanism in the pathway between purpose in life and the better health outcomes associated with it.

articles.title: Political mental health is distinct from mental health and has unique political correlates
articles.authors: Delaney Peterson; Gijs Schumacher; Frederic R. Hopp; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Politics is associated with a range of negative mental and physical health problems. Some work considers how  MH disorders are associated with politics. Others, study to what extent there are mental ill-health symptoms people attribute to politics. We contend directly with why a focus on mental (ill) health attributed to politics is necessary in the study of MH and politics and examine 1) to what extent measures specific to the domain of politics are conceptually distinct from general measures and 2) to what extent domain-specific measures demonstrate a different pattern of association to political correlates. We test and compare the construct and predictive validity of "political mental health" (PMH) and MH in two pre-registered samples in the Netherlands. We find PMH is uni-dimensional and conceptually distinct, but related, to MH and that PMH has stronger associations to relevant political correlates -such as conspiracy mentality and news aversion- and explains unique variance above and beyond a MH measure. We end with suggestions for future work on MH and politics that include the use domain-specific PMH and conclude that PMH has both clinical and political implications.

articles.title: Art as a Bridge Between Brains? A Study of Artist and Viewer Emotion Communication in Abstract Drawing using fNIRS Hyperscanning
articles.authors: Corinna Kühnapfel; Theresa Rahel Demmer; Tao Liu; Helmut Leder; Matthew Pelowski
articles.abstract: Art has often been suggested to evoke shared emotional and empathetic connections between artists and their recipients. However, to-date, there is little empirical research on whether emotions are actually transmitted through art, especially between viewers and artists. Even rarer: can art actually "bridge" both parties' brains? We introduced a paradigm assessing inter-brain synchrony between artists and viewers via functional Near Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning. A cohort of 19 non-artistically trained participants made four abstract drawings, each expressing one target emotion (happiness, pride, fear, anger). The drawing process was filmed and brain activity recorded over affective and cognitive empathy/theory of mind-related cortical regions. A sub-set of the resulting videos (two by each artist, balanced for positive/negative valence) were then viewed by a new cohort of (N = 28) participants while their own brain activity was measured over the same regions and with the task of identifying the target emotion and rating the quality and expressivity of the drawings and difficulty of the recognition task. Behavioral results suggested that all viewers could recognize intended emotions above chance, although with inter-viewer and inter-artwork/artist differences. At the intra-brain level, we found a significant relation between viewers' successful emotion recognition and lower activity in their rIFG as well as between viewers' subjective ratings of task difficulty and drawing expressiveness and activities in viewers' and artists' mPFC and IPL. At the inter-brain level, we found a notable relation between higher coherence between both brains over bilateral lIPL regions and viewers' ratings of lower subjective difficulty in the task. We also detected a positive relation between the artists' ratings of the expressivity of their artworks and higher inter-brain coherence over the rIFG and ATL areas, providing first evidence for an artwork to indeed lead to shared activity patterns between brains.

articles.title: Exploring Domain-Specific Pathways to Resilience in Adolescents: The Role of Executive Functioning
articles.authors: Ranjani Nadarajan; Guillaume Elgbeili; Irina Pokhvisneva; Justin Russotti; Hannah Swerbenski; Patricia P Silveira; Kieran J. O’Donnell; Jennie G. Noll; Ian Gotlib; Michael J Meaney
articles.abstract:
Objective:
Despite the significant risks associated with early life adversity (ELA), there is considerable individual variation in functioning, suggesting the operation of resilience mechanisms. We propose that executive functioning (EF) contributes to resilience following early life adversity (ELA); in this study we examined the mediating role of EF in the associations between ELA and body mass index (BMI), and psychological and academic functioning. 

Method: 
Leveraging data from adolescent girls in the High Adversity (n = 316) and Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD; n = 2533) cohorts, we examined whether total EF problems mediated the associations between ELA and the three outcomes. We then investigated if the two EF indices, Behavioural Regulation and Metacognition differentially mediated the associations between ELA and the three outcomes. 

Results: 
Total EF problems mediated the associations between ELA and BMI z-scores, emotional/behavioural problems, and academic performance in both cohorts. In the High Adversity cohort, both EF indices (Behavioural Regulation and Metacognition) significantly mediated associations between ELA and emotional/behavioural problems and academic performance, but not BMI z-scores. In the ABCD cohort, the Metacognition Index significantly mediated the associations between ELA and BMI z-scores, emotional/behavioural problems and academic performance, whereas the Behavioural Regulation Index mediated only the association between ELA and emotional/behavioural problems.

Conclusion:
Findings indicate that EF may be a potent intervention target for promoting resilience in broad populations.

articles.title: Longitudinal event‑sampling dataset of football fans across five countries during the 2024 European championship
articles.authors: Hannes M. Petrowsky; Yannik A. Escher; Lea Boecker; Kathi Diel; NA; Meikel Neumann; Danna Oomen; Leonie Schwarz; Marie-Annik Strauch; Marcel Weber
articles.abstract: This dataset was collected during the UEFA EURO football championship in 2024. It provides match-contingent experience sampling data, including (a) individual-level variables such as life satisfaction, (b) interpersonal variables such as prosocial intent, and (c) broader societal variables such as political trust. The data points are nested in a sample of N = 1,012 individuals from five countries (England, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland). Using an event-sampling method with four to eight measurement waves (depending on how far the national team progressed in the tournament), we captured time-sensitive fluctuations in a total of m = 30 variables in response to the national team’s objective (i.e., win, draw, loss) and perceived success. In addition, the dataset contains moderating variables including Big-5 personality traits, conspiracy and free-will beliefs, or alcohol consumption and betting behaviors, and detailed match-specific data (e.g., shots on target, yellow cards, attendance). Our data descriptor portrays the methodological approach, data collection procedures, and available variables, and outlines how the data may be used for future research.

articles.title: Shared Human Symbolic Cognition Across Time and Culture
articles.authors: Yuxi Chu; Xingcan Chen; Yanchao Bi
articles.abstract: Humans uniquely externalize ideas through abstract visual symbols. Although symbols are ubiquitous across human cultures and history, the cognitive basis of symbolic meaning remains unclear. We tested whether human symbolic interpretation is supported by shared cognitive tendencies that allow convergence across individuals, cultures, and historical periods without shared conventions. We collected 40,416 open-ended interpretations from 1,637 participants in China and the United States for 242 historical symbols spanning different cultural contexts and over 40,000 years. Participants converged on similar interpretations, with convergence predicting independently established meanings. This effect generalized across cultures and historical periods. In contrast, vision models trained on natural images failed to reproduce human interpretations, indicating that symbolic understanding cannot be reduced to general-purpose visual capacities. Instead, humans appear to rely on stable cognitive principles that map abstract forms onto conceptual representations. These results help explain how symbols emerge, stabilize, and persist across generations.

articles.title: Effects of Ultra-short Offline States on Item-level Verbal Memory
articles.authors: Erin J. Wamsley; Justin Bret Barron; Will Livingston
articles.abstract:
Memory is consolidated during “offline” states of reduced attention to the external stimulus environment, including sleep and resting wakefulness. While consolidation is usually studied on a timescale of hours to days, accumulating evidence suggests that organisms also transiently go offline for very short durations during wakefulness, on a timescale of seconds. Here, we asked how going offline during the intertrial intervals of a verbal memory task affects memory. Participants encoded eight lists of 20 words, during which we continuously recorded high density EEG, pupillometry, RTs, and occasional reports of participants’ subjective focus of attention. Using these multimodal data, we applied our previously published methods to define whether participants were “online” or “offline” just prior to and following the time each individual word was presented. As in prior studies, we found evidence that participants fluctuated between three distinct states during the task, which we term “online” (high EEG delta and theta, larger pupil diameter), “offline1” (high EEG alpha, smaller pupil diameter), and “offline2” (high EEG slow oscillation, smaller pupil diameter). As
anticipated, encoding was superior when participants were online just prior to word presentation. But contrary to our hypotheses, entering an offline state just after word presentation did not improve memory. These observations are discussed in light of memory consolidation theory, including recent evidence of “micro-offline” consolidation in the motor domain.

articles.title: Determining Learner-Specific Prompt Type and Prompt-Fading Procedures for Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles.authors: Ashley R. Kemmerer; Jason Vladescu; Tina M. Sidener; Ruth DeBar; Marlesha C. Bell
articles.abstract: It is widely recognized that individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often require individualized educational programming. However, only a few studies have evaluated using an assessment to identify the most efficient and effective instructional components for individual learners. We replicated and extended Seaver and Bourret (2014) by conducting prompt-type and prompt-fading assessments with two adults with ASD to identify the most efficient prompt type (model, vocal-gestural, or full physical) and prompt-fading procedure (progressive prompt delay, most-to-least, or least-to-most). Following these assessments, we compared the most and least efficient procedures while evaluating whether the assessment results generalized to additional skill types. We also compared the assessment results to those of a decision-making tool, the Systematic Worksheet for the Evaluation of Effective Prompting Strategies (SWEEPS; Cowan et al., 2023). The most efficient prompt type was learner-specific, whereas both participants learned most efficiently using a progressive prompt delay. These outcomes were replicated across additional functional skills and showed clear differences between the most and least efficient procedures. The assessment results were also consistent with the SWEEPS.

articles.title: Pregnant Preconceptions: Experiences of Social Monitoring during Pregnancy
articles.authors: Michelle Ann Kline; Lora Adair; Kenzie Hanson; Heidi Colleran
articles.abstract: Pregnancy is highly visible, and subject to gendered, classed, and racialised expectations. It is also characterised by frequently changing health and wellness recommendations, and cultural narratives regarding 'perfect motherhood'. This paper explores the role of social monitoring—defined as intervention or interruption during daily activities to influence behaviour—on the experience of pregnancy. This article examines who engages in social monitoring; on what topics; how these are valanced (hostile/ benevolent sexism); style of delivery (e.g., advice, help, or constraint) and targets (e.g., race/ethnicity, age, or marital status of the pregnant person); and how pregnant people respond. Participants (n = 205, M age = 37, SD age = 10) were recruited through social media and Prolific, were English-speaking and had experienced at least 12 weeks of pregnancy. Responses were deductively coded using nVivo. We find that socially senior women (mothers, mothers-in-law) are frequently named as intervenors, and that easily observable behaviours (e.g., exercise, food and drink, body or weight) are frequent topics of intervention. While the most common response to monitoring was to persist rather than change their behaviour, some respondents described withdrawing to avoid further intervention. Interventions contain both hostile and benevolent sexism, with Black women reporting a higher ratio of hostility than did other race/ethnic groups. These findings have implications for the social connectedness and mental health of pregnant people and highlight the role of shame and judgment in creating 'no win' situations for mothers-to-be.

articles.title: Do depression stigma and literacy differ between military personnel and the general population? Evidence from a matched comparison of the German Armed Forces (Bundeswehr) and the general population
articles.authors: Caroline Allenhof; Hanna Reich; Andreas Czaplicki; Anna-Lena Nadine Jasmin Leimberger; Jil Zippelius; Annika Heer; Ulrich Hegerl; Gerd Dieter Willmund
articles.abstract:
Objective: Military personnel (MP) are at increased risk of mental health problems yet help-seeking remains low. Depression stigma and literacy are potential barriers to help-seeking, but comparative data between MP and the general population (GP) are limited. This study compared depression stigma and literacy between Bundeswehr MP and the GP and examined sociodemographic and occupational correlates of stigma and literacy.
Methods: Baseline data from operational military personnel (OMP) and military university affiliates (MUA, combined n = 1,964) were compared with participants from representative GP surveys (n = 15,535) matched using propensity scores for age, gender, and education. Depression stigma and literacy were assessed using validated scales and analyzed with multiple regression.
Results:  OMP reported lower personal and perceived stigma than the GP (p ≤ .030), whereas MUA did not differ from the GP in stigma, and neither military group differed from the GP in depression literacy. Mid-aged MP showed lower depression literacy (p < .05). Lower education and lack of contact with depression were associated with higher personal stigma and lower depression literacy in both MP and GP. Personal experience with depression was associated with higher perceived stigma, whereas contact via family/friends/work was associated with higher depression literacy (p ≤ .019). Within the military, lower-ranked and never-deployed personnel reported higher personal stigma (p ≤ .006) and lower literacy (p = .047).
Conclusions: Depression stigma was not higher among MP than in the GP. Interventions should target mid-aged, lower-ranked, and never-deployed personnel, as well as lower-educated individuals without depression contact.

articles.title: Academic dishonesty and questionable research practices in final thesis writing
articles.authors: Lenka Vargová; Marcel Martončik; Gabriel Baník; Artem Buts; Pavol Kačmár; Matus Adamkovic
articles.abstract: Final theses represent a substantial but relatively overlooked form of academic knowledge production. This study provides a descriptive and exploratory insight into academic dishonesty and questionable research practices in thesis writing among N = 1,007 Slovak higher-education graduates who defended a bachelor’s, master’s, rigorous, or doctoral thesis between 2012 and 2024. Participants reported on thesis characteristics, supervision, institutional expectations, psychological and contextual factors, and engagement in dishonest practices such as plagiarism, blind referencing, selective reporting, HARKing, ghostwriting, and data manipulation and fabrication. Although participants generally reported high ethical standards and low intentions to cheat, self-reported engagement in several dishonest practices was not negligible. Academic dishonesty was most consistently associated with neutralizing attitudes, more lenient moral standards, and external pressure, whereas thesis-related characteristics played a comparatively minor role. The findings suggest that academic dishonesty in thesis writing is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon shaped by both individual justifications and contextual pressures. Effective prevention requires a multilevel strategy that simultaneously addresses malleable contextual factors such as supervision, institutional expectations, and peer norms, together with the gradual formation of ethical attitudes and moral identity.

articles.title: A Sequence Sensitive Model of Encoding Precision
articles.authors: Michael Aristodemou; José C. García Alanis; Anna-Lena Schubert; Rogier Kievit
articles.abstract: Canonical visual encoding models do not incorporate the temporal structure of tasks, despite memory performance in real-life contexts almost invariably operating within sequentially structured activities. To address this gap, we developed a Sequence Sensitive model of visual encoding and compared its ability to explain the structure of fluctuations in encoding precision and recognition speed to two established resource-based models of visual encoding, the Population Coding model and the Variable Precision model. We use Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling to formalize the dynamic relationship between a neural proxy of encoding precision and recognition speed, as predicted by all three models. We compared the three resource-based models by fitting them to data from a large sample of 142 participants who completed 100 trials of a short-term memory task, the Sternberg task, while their neural activity was recorded using an electroencephalogram. Our results show that the Sequence Sensitive model outperforms canonical candidates in the context of understanding performance on sequential trial tasks. However, a visual comparison of the model-implied and observed values shows that the three resource-based models only explain a moderate portion of the observed variance. Thus, we should aim to integrate sequential effects into richer and more comprehensive models that incorporate additional features of working memory, such as the interaction between encoding and retrieval processes.

articles.title: Voices in the head: A population-level map of inner-speech modes and agency
articles.authors: Keisuke Suzuki; Hideyuki Takahashi
articles.abstract: Inner-speech research documents striking individual diversity through descriptive phenomenology, self-report questionnaires, and extreme phenotypes, yet prior studies typically sample a few hundred respondents, and no design has mapped how the major modes co-occur or trade off at population scale. We addressed this gap with a video-based online survey (clean N = 5,289): respondents rated seven inner-speech types across three scenarios, alongside agency and sensory-modality self-reports; to our knowledge, it is the largest survey to map this co-occurrence. The study is exploratory: we chart the space's shape rather than test effects, and that shape is continuous and voice-led. The 21-dimensional rating space is a continuous mixture rather than discrete categories, organized into a text family and a voice pair with own voice and visual imagery as standalone axes; reproducible profiles emerge only in the lower-dimensional sensory-modality subspace. The principal opposition is own voice versus visual imagery, not text versus imagery, refining dual-coding theory: only the phonological half of the verbal code opposes imagery, while the orthographic half is near-orthogonal. Own voice also forms an axis independent of the other-voice pair, and the two carry opposite-signed agency associations that are small, as expected for a single item, but consistent in sign. Because the agency and voice items share self/other wording, we treat continuity with sub-clinical voice-hearing as a hypothesis. Unsupervised topic modeling of 1,903 free-text descriptions further corroborates this voice-led organization. These coordinates provide a reference map for idiographic and clinical studies of inner-voice experience.

articles.title: From Clusters to Compositions: Fixed-Frame Archetypal Analysis of the Big Five
articles.authors: David Midgley; Jason Rentfrow; Jeff Potter; Samuel D. Gosling
articles.abstract:
Person-centered psychology has primarily used exploratory discovery algorithms, such as latent
profile analysis and cluster analysis, to identify population subgroups (e.g., “Resilient”). These
methods face several well-documented limitations: identified profiles vary across datasets
(sample dependence), the number of profiles relies on ambiguous stopping rules, and forcing
continuous personality configurations into discrete categories can conflate the measurement
granularity of Likert lattices with genuine structure. In response, we introduce fixed-frame
archetypal analysis (FFAA), which represents each individual as a continuous compositional
mixture relative to fixed theoretical extrema (the absolute corners of the Big Five hypercube)
using closed-form multilinear interpolation. The method contributes at two levels. For the
individual respondent, FFAA is a lossless reparameterization of trait scores into a fixed, sample-
independent coordinate system, providing (1) fixed profile definitions, (2) high-resolution
measurement of configural differences, and (3) computational scalability. Across respondents,
because compositions are nonlinear functions of the traits, averaging them encodes the
covariation among traits that marginal averages do not retain. We illustrate the individual-level
properties through simulation studies and establish a normative baseline from over 10 million
respondents; at the aggregate level, these data characterize the maturity principle across the adult
lifespan not as discrete stages but as a continuous geometric migration that is broadly similar
across regions. We propose that moving from “profile discovery” to “compositional
measurement” offers a mathematically grounded approach to person-centered psychology,
though establishing predictive validity and extending FFAA to other personality measures remain
important next steps.

articles.title: Mental Health Clinicians' Knowledge, Attitudes, Practices and Barriers regarding Diet's Effects on Depression: a Systematic Review of Observational Studies
articles.authors: David Morgan; James Sorensen; Arriel Vaz; Tetyana Rocks; Delyse Tien; Leo Chen; Heidi Staudacher
articles.abstract: Depression is a leading cause of disease burden worldwide with significant interest in new therapeutic approaches. Nutritional psychiatry is emerging as an increasingly evidence-based therapeutic tool. However, its incorporation into mainstream clinical practice has lagged. Key to understanding and addressing this lag is the clinician’s experience, with few studies having explored this area to date. This systematic review sets out to identify and synthesise the available literature on mental health clinicians’ (MHCs’) knowledge, attitudes, practice and barriers (KAPB) regarding diet’s role in depression. A systematic search across 5 databases (MEDLINE, Emcare, PsycInfo, CINAHL and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews) was conducted on April 3rd, 2026. Eligible studies sampled MHCs working with adults and explored the KAPB domains relating to diet’s role in depression. 12 publications representing 10 unique studies from around the world were included. Results consistently found low levels of training but high interest in further education. Attitudes and practices varied across studies, ranging from scepticism to strong support, with there being a predominance of support in more recent studies. Clinicians incorporating nutritional psychiatry into practice often reported low confidence or perceived expertise. Recommended approaches included Mediterranean-style dietary patterns, adherence to national dietary guidelines, and nutritional supplements, most frequently vitamin D, folic acid, B vitamins and omega-3. The main reported barriers to practice included insufficient training, concerns about professional scope and doubts about client interest and adherence. Overall, few studies were eligible and many were at risk of selection and reporting bias. Together they nonetheless provided a useful initial overview of many key and relevant themes. Findings highlighted the need for greater integration of nutritional psychiatry into mental health education, professional development, and service delivery. Future efforts should focus on localised implementation studies and interventions addressing identified barriers to practice.

articles.title: Phenomenological-control framing of suggestion-based interventions: a testable hypothesis for acceptability and implementation in psychiatric care
articles.authors: Adrian Sanger; Tadeusz Pietras
articles.abstract: This Hypothesis and Theory article draws on a targeted, non-systematic synthesis of relevant literature and does not report new empirical data. Suggestion-based interventions show clinical promise across several medical conditions, yet their uptake in routine care remains limited. Psychiatry may be a particularly informative context in which to examine framing-related barriers because treatment engagement, perceived agency, trust, acceptability, and appropriateness may be especially sensitive to how an intervention is described and understood. In response to these concerns, the article considers whether selected suggestion-based interventions could be presented through a phenomenological-control framing. Phenomenological control refers here to a patient-side capacity for the goal-directed regulation of subjective experience, whereas a phenomenological-control framing uses that capacity as the explanatory rationale for the intervention. The intervention itself remains a clinical procedure involving structured suggestions. The central hypothesis is that, relative to a hypnotic framing, a phenomenological-control framing may influence implementation-relevant responses without implying greater clinical efficacy. Patient-level predictions concern perceived agency, concerns about loss of control, acceptability, appropriateness, and willingness to engage. Provider-level predictions concern scientific credibility, appropriateness, and intentions to recommend, refer, adopt, or seek training. These predictions are conditional and may vary across individuals and contexts.

articles.title: Idiographic Memory Modelling in ACT-R Using Alternating Maximum Likelihood Estimation
articles.authors: Maarten van der Velde; Thomas Wilschut; Hedderik van Rijn; Andrea Stocco
articles.abstract: Performance on memory tasks varies systematically between individuals and within individuals over time. However, computational models of memory are often fitted at the group level or summarise performance in a single parameter, potentially obscuring the distinct cognitive processes that give rise to this variation. Here we present a likelihood-based procedure for fitting the multi-parameter ACT-R declarative memory model at the level of the individual. Using this method, we jointly estimate five participant-level or idiographic parameters, each capturing a distinct component of memory performance, together with item-level variation in memorability. A parameter recovery study on synthetic data shows that these participant- and item-level parameters are jointly identifiable from realistic amounts of data on a typical spaced repetition memory task, requiring only about 40-90 observations of response accuracy and speed per participant. We demonstrate the method on a dataset of individuals with mild cognitive impairment and age-matched healthy controls, finding that mild cognitive impairment is marked by differences in three parameters signifying accelerated forgetting, less efficient memory retrieval, and general psychomotor slowing. These results show that the method can successfully decompose observed performance on a memory task into separable, individually interpretable components. More broadly, this work contributes to the development of fine-grained idiographic memory models that can capture dynamics in memory performance both between and within individuals, with applications in experimental research and applied settings, such as computational phenotyping for clinical diagnosis.

articles.title: chatPsych: An Artificial Intelligence Interface for Human-AI Interaction Research
articles.authors: Oliver Lack; Carolyn Semmler
articles.abstract: Human computer interaction research remains largely ungeneralisable and popular methods fail to adequately represent the rapidly evolving systems in society. chatPsych aims to provide the research community with access to a generalisable method that facilitates rich, representative human-AI interaction contexts. chatPsych is a novel research tool for building and deploying studies that focus on interaction with frontier AI models. The system comprises programmable surveys surrounding interactions with a chat/assistant interface that connects participants to a specified model with researcher tailored parameters. The aesthetics and features of the interface resemble prevalent chat/assistant technologies and data from interactions/surveys are scraped and locally downloadable from the researcher dashboard GUI. This GUI also allows programming and randomisation of varying AI agents to participant interactions. These agents can be modified via prompt engineering, model hyperparameters, model selection, moderated responses/prompts/captures/buttons, and more. Although chatPsych may be adapted by technically inclined investigators, it offers extensive features and deployment instructions for non-technical researchers. The system uses standardised API connections to an extensive range of model providers. Its standalone nature provides accessibility/customisability for many study designs at scale online and in lab-based settings. We introduce and validate this tool as an open-source codebase for the research community. chatPsych is available at https://chatpsych.org/.

articles.title: Support for climate and biodiversity policies differs across cultural worldviews in Japan
articles.authors: Aya Takagi; Ryosuke Nakadai
articles.abstract: Social polarisation poses a major challenge to collective climate action. In this context, biodiversity conservation, when aligned with climate objectives, may face less worldview-driven resistance than direct climate policies. However, the links between values of nature and wider cultural worldviews remain poorly understood. Here we show, using a nationwide survey (N = 1,133) in Japan, how cultural worldviews relate to risk perception and environmental policy support.  Individuals with hierarchical worldviews perceived climate change risks as lower and tended to be less supportive of climate change measures than individuals with more egalitarian worldviews. Yet these negative associations were weaker for perceived biodiversity loss risks and for support for climate change-related biodiversity conservation measures, and no direct association was found for stand-alone biodiversity conservation measures. General scientific knowledge was positively associated with support for biodiversity conservation measures, including those related to climate change. These associations between cultural worldviews and policy support differed across climate and biodiversity policy domains.

articles.title: Undue Influence as Dynamic Constraint of Agency-Space: A Mechanism-Level Theory of Conscious Agency Under Control
articles.authors: T. Dawson Woodrum
articles.abstract: Prior theories of thought reform, coercive persuasion, bounded choice, coercive control, and undue influence have made enduring contributions by identifying tactics, environments, interpersonal patterns, and ideological conditions through which people may be controlled. Their principal strength is descriptive: they name the architecture of control. This article addresses a different theoretical problem: how that architecture becomes psychologically consequential inside the person. I propose Agency-Space Theory, a process-level account of undue influence as dynamic constraint of conscious agency. Agency-space is the structured field within which a person experiences possible thought, meaning, relationship, identity, and action. Undue influence occurs when external conditions narrow this field so that externally preferred outcomes become internally experienced as necessity, loyalty, morality, safety, or survival. The theory makes four contributions. First, it explains how control becomes internal constraint. Second, it distinguishes behavior from agency-space, explaining how voluntary-appearing compliance can coexist with constrained agency. Third, it predicts narrative and experiential entailments of narrowing, including reduced perceived alternatives, externally anchored meaning, altered self-other boundaries, temporal narrowing, compliance-as-necessity, demoralization, and compartmentalized self-models. Fourth, it specifies focused complex-adaptive-systems implications: feedback loops may stabilize constrained configurations; attractor-like patterns may deepen over time; path dependence may make earlier compliance alter later possibilities; and hysteresis may persist after exit. Cognitive dissonance, demoralization, and dissociation are treated as local processes within this broader account rather than as competing global explanations. The result is not another inventory of control tactics, but a theory of how control environments transform conscious agency over time.

articles.title: Exploring the role of identity fusion and group identification in predicting parochialism amongst Indonesian Islamic groups
articles.authors: Christopher Michael Kavanagh; Susilo Wibisono; Rohan Kapitány; Whinda Yustisia; Idhamsyah Eka Putra; Harvey Whitehouse
articles.abstract: Indonesia is home to more Muslims than any other country in the world, yet the interpretation of the faith differs between groups, communities, and individuals. Here we examine how the diversity of beliefs and practices among Indonesian Muslims relate to group bonding and parochialism. Specifically, we examine the predictive power of two distinct types of group alignment, group identification and identity fusion, among politically unaﬀiliated Indonesian Muslims and individuals associated with two prominent Islamic organizations: the explicitly political and Islamist Prosperity and Justice Party (PKS) and the more moderate Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), the largest religious organization in Indonesia. We found that PKS members were more fused to relevant group identities than NU members or unaﬀiliated Indonesian Muslims. Across all three groups, identity fusion was associated with parochial outcomes, including expressed willingness to carry out extreme pro-group actions, but group identification was the stronger predictor. We discuss how religious beliefs and practices shape parochial attitudes, as well as the implications for theoretical models linking fusion, identification, threat, and extreme behaviour.

articles.title: Visual Pattern Completion of Occluded Objects Promotes Robust Visual Learning
articles.authors: Jennifer Gove; David E. Huber; Rosemary Cowell
articles.abstract: Recognizing a partially occluded object is effortless and automatic: visual cortex fills in the missing parts to infer a recognizable whole. We tested whether part-to-whole visual pattern completion constitutes not just a retrieval operation, but also a learning mechanism. Participants studied whole objects, after which each object was assigned either to retrieval practice, cued by a circular aperture offering a “peephole” view, or to restudy. At final test, retrieval-practiced (peephole-cued) objects were better remembered than restudied objects – a visual testing effect. The task eliminated the utility of conceptual information, suggesting that this testing effect occurs without semantic mediation, contrary to prominent theories. Critically, when retrieval no longer required pattern completion—retrieval without a peephole cue—the testing effect disappeared. Thus, we report a non-semantically mediated visual testing effect driven by occlusion-induced pattern completion. We suggest that visual pattern completion supports not only occluded object recognition, but also robust visual learning.

articles.title: Does Carbon Pricing Outperform Command-and-Control Regulation? Firm-Level Evidence from Korea’s Dual Regulatory Framework
articles.authors: Pyung Kim
articles.abstract: This study exploits South Korea’s unique dual-policy, in which an emissions trading scheme (ETS) and a command-and-control program (Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel, to compare carbon pricing with prescriptive regulation at the firm level. Using a difference-in-differences design on firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2022, I find that ETS-regulated firms reduced energy use by 5.8% to 8.8% and carbon emissions by 7.3% to 8.5% relative to TMS firms, while effects on carbon intensity were not robust. These reductions were strongest in the more market-oriented phases of the ETS, which featured allowance auctioning and benchmark-based allocation, pointing to the importance of incentive-based policy design.

articles.title: Projecting Intergenerational Family Structures  over the Life Course:  Empirical and Simulated Populations in Norway
articles.authors: Bettina Hünteler; Diego Alburez-Gutierrez
articles.abstract: Much existing research in the demography of kinship focuses on quantifying the number and characteristics of living kin, such as age and sex. We know less about which intergenerational family structures individuals experience throughout their life – for example, when and how long they are parents, children or experience overlap of multiple family generations – although this is important because such trajectories are heterogeneous, potentially producing inequalities in kinship availability across the life. We use simulated micro-level data to project generational placement trajectories for life courses of the complete population of Norway born 1960 and 2000. Our microsimulations use age-specific fertility and mortality rates from 1846 to 2100. First, we benchmark projected trajectories for the 1960 cohort against observed trajectories from empirical register data from 1960 to 2019. Second, we project full life-course trajectories, from age 0 to 100, for the 1960 and 2000 cohorts. Results from sequence analysis show that generational placement trajectories efficiently capture individual-level heterogeneity in intergen-erational kin availability and that results based on our simulated populations largely match those from empirical data. Over cohorts, typical generational placement trajectories will likely become more stable but “thinner”, with later (and shorter) demographic “(double) sandwiching” and increasingly frequent “fading family lines.” The analysis paves the path toward results on a global level and including projections for the future.

articles.title: The Weight of Precedent: Parties, Institutions, and Executive Norms
articles.authors: Daniel A. N. Goldstein; Collin Thomas Schumock
articles.abstract: Political executives often adhere to informal traditions established by their predecessors. Yet, without legal backing, elites have incentives to violate norms for political gain. Under what conditions do constraining executive norms persist and when are they abandoned? We address this question by using an infinite horizon formal model to analyze the maintenance of executive norms. We identify intra-party accountability and variation in patience among actors within the same party as significant for norm maintenance. We also detail how expectations about the expected behavior of out-of-power parties shape the willingness to violate norms while in office. The insights from the model enable us to classify a number of executive norms according to their fragility and to examine the trajectory of one norm in-depth: the two-term tradition of the American presidency. Our findings shed light on how informal institutions regulate executive behavior and advance our understanding of institutional stability and erosion.

articles.title: Indirect Influence: How Elite Attacks on Information Providers Affect Public Opinion Formation
articles.authors: Erik Peterson; Allison Michelle Nam Archer; Kishan Bhakta; SHO IZUMISAWA
articles.abstract: Attacks from politicians can dramatically reduce public trust in sources of expertise and information. We consider the consequences of such criticism and argue that by shaping which information providers their supporters consider credible, politicians can exert indirect influence over public opinion formation. In two survey experiments that link elite criticism of the media to other outcomes, we show politicians who discredit a media outlet cause their supporters to avoid the targeted news source and perceive more bias in its coverage. Partisan attacks also reduce the subsequent effect of the news source's coverage on public opinion, although people are unable to fully discount information from sources they deem untrustworthy due to this rhetoric. Looking beyond direct means of elite influence such as positional cues and policy arguments, we show how harming the reputations of information providers allows politicians to indirectly influence the views of their supporters.

articles.title: Mandatory AI Disclosure Sorts Products into Launch Failure: Evidence from Steam
articles.authors: Kenny Ching
articles.abstract: Platforms increasingly require firms to disclose when products incorporate generative artificial intelligence (AI). Existing evidence largely asks whether such disclosure changes consumer demand; we show that a complementary question—where demand is lost—is at least as important. Using a cross-section of 799 visual-novel games on Steam released early enough to observe a complete 90-day post-release window—of which 22% carry a platform-mandated AI-use disclosure—we show that the consumer response to AI disclosure is concentrated almost entirely on the extensive margin. Disclosed games are roughly twice as likely to obtain no early traction at all: the rate of zero day-30 reviews rises from 5.0% to 9.0%, an odds ratio of 2.14. Among games that do gain an audience, by contrast, the rate of subsequent review accumulation is statistically indistinguishable by disclosure status, and the continuous accumulation penalty is not robust to controls. Disclosed games that are reviewed receive ratings about six percentage points lower. The market response to disclosure is therefore not a uniform discount applied to every product, but a bimodal pattern: a higher probability of failing to launch, and modestly lower satisfaction among survivors. We discuss implications for the design of mandatory disclosure more broadly: when a label can determine whether a product is seen at all, the welfare consequences of disclosure differ sharply depending on whether it gently discounts demand or sorts products into launch failure, and on the producer incentives it sets in motion.

articles.title: High resolution measures of preference-based local segregation for the United States, 2018-2023
articles.authors: Jiwon Jang; Dylan Shane Connor; Peter Rogerson; Daoqin Tong
articles.abstract: Neighborhood segregation is a strong driver of disparities in human well-being, yet traditional measures largely ignore the segregation experienced beyond residential neighborhoods. Recent human mobility-based measures have advanced this field by quantifying segregated mobility patterns when choosing travel destinations, but they are often confounded by spatial exposure (i.e., the demographic diversity of the neighborhoods locally reachable from one’s residence) rather than a behavioral preference for similarity. Without adjusting for this baseline exposure, such metrics largely act as proxies for the local residential environment, conflating limited demographic diversity in surrounding areas with active travel decisions to neighborhoods similar to one’s own. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Community Connectivity (CO-CONNECT) dataset, combining billions of anonymized cellphone location records with census tract-level socio-demographic attributes (2018-2023). The dataset operationalizes the Spatial Preference in Local Interaction (SPLIT) index, a local measure of segregation that quantifies the extent to which residents travel to socio-demographically similar neighborhoods, adjusted for the demographic similarity of surrounding neighborhoods. This framework explicitly separates travel decisions that exacerbate group-based segregation from segregation attributable to demographic composition alone, providing a high-resolution picture of mobility-based segregation and its temporal trends across the United States.

articles.title: The Suburb Disruption Cycle and Dorsett’s Law of Suburban Succession: A Theoretical Model of Residential Turnover and Suburban Reinvention
articles.authors: Mark Dorsett
articles.abstract:
This paper proposes the Suburb Disruption Cycle as a theoretical model for explaining
suburban transformation as a patterned process of disruption, reorganisation and
residential succession. Existing accounts of suburban change often emphasise particular
dimensions of transformation, including decline, gentrification, densification, migration,
financialisation, post-suburbanisation and symbolic revaluation. This paper synthesises
these dimensions into an eight-stage causal sequence: Current Residents, Disruption,
Housing Form, Affordability, Reputation, Business Ecology, Resident Turnover and New
Residents. From this sequence, the paper derives Dorsett’s Law of Suburban Succession:
sustained disruption within or upon a suburb produces residential succession when it
reorganises housing form, affordability, reputation and business ecology. The law is
advanced as a conditional sociological proposition rather than a deterministic claim. Its
purpose is to explain how new resident orders are produced through cumulative material,
economic, symbolic and commercial change. The paper develops the model conceptually
and applies it to St Kilda, Victoria, during its Riviera of Victoria life cycle from 1860 to
1910. The case demonstrates how transport access, gold-rush wealth, land speculation
and financial crisis contributed to housing transformation, rising exclusivity, reputational
elevation, leisure-oriented business development and the emergence of a new elite seaside
resident order. The paper contributes a middle-range theory of suburban reinvention that
can guide future historical, comparative and empirical research into suburban succession.

articles.title: When Are Democracies Under Strain? Supranational Economic Integration, Financial Crises, and Satisfaction with Democracy
articles.authors: Rubén Ruiz-Rufino
articles.abstract: Why does external financial support erode democratic satisfaction in some countries but leave it intact in others? This article argues that the answer lies in the depth of supranational economic integration. Where integration is limited, conditionality releases information about government performance: elections retain their accountability function and democratic satisfaction remains stable or recovers. Where integration is deep, conditionality releases systemic information: citizens learn that elections are uninformative about future policy direction, and satisfaction falls. This integration gradient hypothesis predicts that the sign, magnitude, and mechanism of conditionality's democratic effects vary continuously with integration depth. Across five cases spanning the continuum --- Colombia and South Korea at the low-integration pole, Hungary at an intermediate position, and the Eurozone and Portugal at the high-integration pole --- the evidence is consistent with the gradient. What appears as contradictory evidence in the literature is the theoretically predicted pattern of a single mechanism at different integration positions.

articles.title: Unexpected Journeys: Russian Migrants Navigating Education and Social Spaces in the European Union
articles.authors: Mariia Daletskaia
articles.abstract: This study aims to identify how recent Russian migrant families navigate the European social space and conceptualize their newly acquired social position. It investigates the educational strategies and social integration of recent Russian middle-class migrant families within the European Union. Utilizing Bourdieu’s theoretical framework of social space and capital, the research explores how these families navigate their new social environments and conceptualize their social positions post-migration. For this qualitative analysis, data collection was conducted using semi-structured in-depth interviews as the primary research technique. The data was then thoroughly processed and analyzed using the tools proposed by Laclau and Mouffe’s discourse theory. The findings reveal that these families were among the select few in the high-income strata in Russia and now experience downward mobility upon relocating to the social space of European countries. Though this group of migrants cannot be fully conceptualized as the Global Middle Class's representatives, their actions align with the aspiration to sustain and elevate their social position. Their incomes may remain constant or even increase, yet they transition from select groups to the European middle class. Although this appears to be downward mobility, it is a strategic move to reinforce the family’s social standing within the global social space.

articles.title: From crime survey items to measurement: Developing the perceived (un)safety scale
articles.authors: Jeanette Melin; Magnus Johansson
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This study examines the ability of a new collection of survey items, the perceived (un)safety scale, to function as a coherent invariant scale. Its secondary aim is to investigate how the perceived (un)safety scale can be used to identify associations with perceived unsafety across groups.
Methods: Employing a cross-sectional psychometric design, data were collected through a postal survey in four Swedish municipal districts, differentiated by size and sociodemographic composition (n = 1,387), and a nationwide panel sample (n = 1,340). With the intention of measuring avoidance behaviours and detours due to fear of crime, the preliminary scale comprised five items. Rasch analysis was used to evaluate these measurements, and regression analyses were conducted to examine associations with individual characteristics.
Results: Initial analyses identified one misfitting item and local dependency between two items. After removing the misfitting item and combining the locally dependent items into a testlet, a unidimensional and invariant scale was obtained. Higher levels of perceived (un)safety were associated with being a woman, being younger, and having a history of victimization.
Conclusions: The perceived (un)safety scale provides a coherent and invariant measure of perceived (un)safety across demographic groups. The scale may be useful for future research, population surveys, and evaluations of interventions aimed at improving safety and reducing fear of crime.

articles.title: When Central Banks Go Green: Public Opinion and Monetary Policy Legitimacy
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth; Anita Mancosu
articles.abstract:
Climate change presents unelected central banks with an acute dilemma: acting on
climate change risks charges of mandate overreach, while failing to act risks charges
of institutional failure. Yet public opinion on green central banking remains un-
studied. We address this gap with two survey experiments in Germany and the
Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that adding environmental condition-
ality to corporate bond purchases significantly increases support for quantitative
easing, suggesting that greening can rehabilitate contested unconventional policies.
A framing experiment reveals that institutional objections about price stability
and democratic legitimacy erode support more than distributive objections about
job losses or asset devaluation, inverting expectations from the climate politics
literature. Respondents who trust the central bank most are paradoxically most
responsive to arguments for and against it. Public trust in delegated institutions
is thus not a blank check; it is a license granted on terms, policed most attentively
by the institution’s own supporters.

articles.title: Safeguards, Strategic Behavior, and Great Power Competition: The IAEA’s Board of Governors as an Instrument of Leverage for Potential Non- Compliers
articles.authors: Ralph Rotte; Victoria Alberty; Andreas Dürholt; René Geiser
articles.abstract:
This paper takes a critical view of the prospective ability of the IAEA to be an essential contributor to a stable
international nuclear order and prevention of nuclear proliferation, given that it is an international governmental
organization. The Agency is considered to be characterized by the ambiguities of a more or less autonomous
bureaucratic and technocratic organization led by the Secretariat. Furthermore, it is considered an
intergovernmental arena of state actors for decision-making on the political consequences of breaking Safeguards
rules with the Boards of Governors as a quasi-upstream body of the UN Security Council. As is typical for IGOs
one can therefore expect it to ultimately be an instrument of states’ foreign policy interests which reflects the
overall situation of the international system and its prevalent power structures and conflicts. Especially in times of
power transition and a revisionist dissolution of an established international order this may lead to rivalling great
powers’ acting according to their strategic priorities and protecting states that fail to fully comply with nuclear
safeguards obligations, instead of providing for effective implementation of non-proliferation measures. As a
consequence, this instrumentalization of the IAEA policy making bodies by leading powers’ strategic interests
might enable unreliable countries to avoid diplomatic pressure or sanctions for clandestine cheating or even to
whitewash their nuclear programs. By looking at the cases of Iran, South Korea, Egypt and Libya, we find that
alliance politics and strategic behavior may indeed hamper the effectiveness of the IAEA as the global nuclear
watchdog. Consequently, at least from a realist and strategic studies perspective, the IAEA and the nuclear nonproliferation
regime face an ever-increasing structural challenge in the current context of aggravating great power
competition.

articles.title: Fragmented Identity, Saffron Strategy: Navigating the Bharatiya Janata Party's Ascendance in Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR) of Assam
articles.authors: Bikash Dihingia; Chuchengfa Gogoi; Pankaj Kumar Sarmah
articles.abstract: The unprecedented rise of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 election to the Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR), erstwhile Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) of Assam, marked a significant development in the region's political landscape, which is historically dominated by the Bodoland People’s Front (BPF), an ethnic political party representing the Bodos. For decades, the BPF exercised near-hegemonic control over the BTC, shaping governance structures and political dialogue through an ethnic-centric approach. The fourth BTR election disrupted this established order and brought in a more competitive and pluralistic political environment. The shift from single-party dominance to an emerging multi-party system not only reconfigured electoral alignments but also contested the institutional and ideological bases of BPF’s authority. This study thoroughly examines the growing dynamics of electoral politics in the BTR, positioning the 2020 election as a decisive departure from conventional patterns of political mobilisation and voter behaviour. It also explores how changing socio-political conditions, including internal differentiations within the Bodo community, generated new opportunities for political contestation. Particular attention is given to the BJP’s strategic interventions, especially its capacity to leverage fragmented ethnic identities and integrate them within a wider electoral framework. Through this analysis, the study intends to advance understanding of shifting political narratives, party competition, and identity negotiations in contemporary Bodoland.

articles.title: E-Commerce Challenges and Opportunities in Turkey: The Cases of Getir and Trendyol
articles.authors: Abd Elaziz Zoabi
articles.abstract: This article explores the challenges and opportunities of e-commerce in Turkey through inducting a comparison between Getir and Trendyol cases. With the fast expansion of digital technologies, e-commerce has reformed consumer habits, business strategies, and the retail landscape. based on secondary data from company reports, industry analysis, and academic studies, this research follows a qualitative case study approach to evaluate how both companies achieved market growth while dealing with operational and regulatory pressures and challenges. Findings reveal that e-commerce platforms create essential opportunities, including consumer convenience, market expansion, and innovation-driven growth. At the same time, they face significant challenges such as high operational costs, supply chain issues, legal and regulatory issues, and economic instability due to current conditions. The analysis shows that Getir’s ultra-fast delivery model enabled early growth but came with sustainability concerns, while Trendyol’s marketplace model ensured greater scalability but faced increasing competition. Overall, the study contributes to understanding how e-commerce businesses in emerging markets adapt strategies to sustain growth within dynamic conditions. It further provides practical insights for policymakers, businesses, and startups on building sustainable, competitive, and consumer-centered e-commerce ecosystems.

articles.title: Lame Duck by Primary: Effects of Electoral Incentives on U.S. House Representatives
articles.authors: Kisoo Kim
articles.abstract: How do electoral incentives motivate representatives to exert effort and shape policy positions? While reelection is widely recognized as representatives' primary motivation in democratic politics, accurately estimating its effects is challenging because representatives self-select into rerunning or retiring decisions. Leveraging legislators’ lame duck status after primary elections, this article estimates how electoral incentives affect U.S. House Representatives. Compiling data from 1955 to 2022, I compare legislators who win primaries and remain motivated for reelection to those who lose and exit the race. Through regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs, I find that primary losers significantly reduce effort-related activities, as evidenced by decreased roll-call participation, bill sponsorship, and voter communication. In contrast, the results show that legislators do not adjust policy positions for reelection; both winners and losers maintain consistent ideological and party-line adherence. These findings illuminate the scope of electoral incentives' effects and contribute to debates on electoral accountability and democratic representation.

articles.title: When Formal Sanctions Synchronize: A Multi-Level Model of Organizational Defensive Escalation
articles.authors: Koichi Hiraoka
articles.abstract:
This paper offers a theoretical account of how internal problem-raising and workplace 
conflict may shift into chains of formal procedures and sanctions. Prior research has 
examined organizational defensiveness through institutional legitimacy, threat-rigidity, 
defensive routines, psychological safety, whistleblower retaliation, and organizational 
silence. These studies have shown that organizations often respond to internal 
disturbance by narrowing attention, reinforcing procedures, and suppressing voice. Less 
attention, however, has been paid to how interactional control at the individual level 
becomes connected with formal organizational procedures at the institutional level. 
To address this issue, the paper reconsiders the Formality–Sanction Loop (FS-Loop) 
as a multi-level process. At the interpersonal level, an individual FS-Loop operates 
through the detection of minor formal deviations, criticism, demands for apology or 
reflection, and confirmation of compliance. Such interactions may reduce the target’s 
capacity to speak or act autonomously. At the organizational level, an institutional 
FS-Loop operates when internal problem-raising is redefined less as a substantive issue 
than as a matter of procedure, documentation, attitude, or order, and is then processed 
through meetings, records, warnings, disciplinary procedures, or reassignment. 
The central argument is that organizational defensive escalation becomes more likely 
when these two loops synchronize. A local judgment that a person is insufficiently 
reflective or in need of correction may support formal organizational procedures, while 
organizational records and sanctions may reinforce the local judgment that the person is 
problematic. Through this mutual reinforcement, the substantive issue recedes into the 
background, while the person’s attitude, procedural compliance, documentary record, 
and willingness to comply become the main focus. 
The paper positions FS-Loop synchronization as a middle-range framework for 
examining harassment, whistleblower retaliation, organizational silence, disciplinary 
procedures, and the erosion of psychological safety. Rather than reducing such cases 
either to individual hostility or institutional failure alone, the model highlights how 
locally reasonable actions may become connected across levels and produce defensive 
closure.

articles.title: India’s Economic Crossroads: Growth, Inequality, Dependency, and the Road Ahead
articles.authors: Devraj Singh
articles.abstract:
India has re‑emerged as one of the world’s fastest‑growing large economies, yet persistent concerns about job quality, inequality, and strategic dependence raise doubts about how far headline growth translates into durable development. 

This paper asks whether India can convert high growth into inclusive, job‑rich, and strategically resilient development in a frontier‑technology era defined by AI, semiconductors, digital public infrastructure, and advanced defence and data‑centre technologies. 

Using a secondary‑data, mixed‑methods design, the study combines national time series, a state‑year panel, and trade and energy‑dependence indicators constructed from official Indian sources (MoSPI, RBI, NITI Aayog, PPAC, TradeStat, NPCI) and major international databases (World Bank, IMF, WID). 

The analysis documents that while real output and fiscal‑backed investment have risen strongly, labour reallocation into high‑productivity manufacturing and modern services remains incomplete, so growth has been output‑rich but only partially employment‑rich across most states.

Official consumption data show substantial poverty reduction, but inequality remains high and multi‑dimensional, with rising top‑end concentration and enduring gaps by state, caste, gender, and employment type. 

External vulnerability is concentrated in oil, electronics, and advanced hardware and software inputs, even as digital public infrastructure and frontier‑tech sectors deepen. 

The paper argues that India’s long‑run challenge is not growth per se but the political‑economy task of aligning structural transformation, capability‑building, and technology‑era industrial and social policy so that high growth yields broad‑based mobility, lower strategic dependence, and stronger, more even state capacity.

articles.title: Genetic Mirroring in Adoptees: Toward a Formal Construct Definition, Nomological Network, and Operationalization Framework
articles.authors: Giulia Suzzi
articles.abstract: Genetic mirroring, the developmentally recurring need to perceive reflected biological similarity in genetically related others, has gained clinical salience as an explanatory framework for the identity experiences of adoptees and donor-conceived individuals. Despite this, the construct lacks the theoretical architecture required for empirical investigation: a precise definition, differentiation from adjacent constructs, and a plausible operationalization pathway. The present paper addresses that gap through four coordinated contributions. First, a formal construct definition is proposed, encompassing three theoretically distinct dimensions: biological salience, embodied discontinuity, and mirroring responsiveness. Second, the construct is situated within a nomological network specifying its hypothesized relationships with established psychological variables, including identity exploration, narrative identity coherence, attachment security, genealogical bewilderment, and physical self-concept. Third, a theoretical case is made for incremental validity over existing frameworks: genetic mirroring is proposed to capture variance in adoptee psychological functioning that neither attachment theory nor narrative identity frameworks can fully account for. Fourth, a preliminary scale structure is proposed as proof of concept. The paper's aim is to transform a clinically emergent construct into a formally theorizable and measurable entity, enabling the empirical program necessary to evaluate its scientific and practical significance.

articles.title: Disproportionate Psychiatric Hospitalization of Black American Adults and the Role of Diagnostic Disparities
articles.authors: Arnold Barnes
articles.abstract: Disproportionate psychiatric hospitalization of Black Americans has been identified as a mental health disparity; however, few national studies have examined this disparity. This article reports on whether Black adults are hospitalized at a percentage higher than their population percentage and diagnostic differences between Black and White adults receiving services in state hospitals and other hospital inpatient settings. A subsample of adults ages 18 to 60 and older (N = 263,943) was drawn from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s 2020 Mental health client-level data set. Univariate analysis found that the percentage of Blacks receiving services in state hospitals and other hospitals exceeded their percentage in the 2020 U.S. population (12%) by 19.7% and 9.5% respectively. Bivariate and regression analysis revealed an association between Black race and diagnoses of schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders in both hospital settings. Approaches for addressing disproportionate hospitalization and diagnostic bias are suggested.

articles.title: Individual characteristics, family environment, and destination language learning: A mixed methods study on newly arrived migrant children in Türkiye and Germany
articles.authors: Abdullah Atmacasoy; Hanife Akar; Ingrid Gogolin
articles.abstract:
As global migration continues to reshape contemporary societies, destination language learning is central to newly arrived migrant children’s inclusion in mainstream education. This mixed methods, cross-cultural comparative study examined how migration-related characteristics and family environment are associated with self-assessed destination language proficiency among newly arrived migrant children in Türkiye and Germany. Drawing on Bronfenbrenner’s ecological model of human development, the study combined survey data from 245 refugee children in Istanbul and 189 newly arrived migrant children in Hamburg with 77 qualitative interviews and 33 hours of classroom observations.

Quantitative data were analyzed using hierarchical and moderated linear regression models, and qualitative data through thematic analysis.
Across both contexts, longer residence in the receiving country and stronger first-language proficiency were associated with higher destination language proficiency, whereas age at migration was not. Prior primary schooling predicted higher destination language proficiency only in Istanbul. Family involvement alone was not associated with destination language proficiency; however, stronger destination language proficiency among mothers and siblings predicted children’s proficiency and strengthened the positive association between family involvement and children’s destination language proficiency. The findings suggest broadly similar trajectories of destination language development across contexts while highlighting the importance of families’ linguistic resources for educational engagement.

articles.title: Governing Epistemic Sustainability: Epistemic Enclosure, Double Concealment, and Knowledge Sovereignty in India's Viksit Bharat 2047
articles.authors: S Anas Ahmad; Mohammad Anas; Abdullah Nouman; Filza Zaki Khan
articles.abstract:
India's Viksit Bharat 2047 framework (2026) and the IndiaAI Mission (2024) conflate compute sovereignty with knowledge sovereignty, embedding India within AI infrastructure whose epistemic consequences existing sustainability governance cannot register. Reading India's AI governance corpus as performative political narratives, the paper identifies the rhetorical operations through which compute capacity is narrated as knowledge sovereignty, and the silences through which epistemic costs are rendered external to the governance frame. 

To name what this discourse cannot see, the paper develops three interlocking concepts, each addressing a different question: what must be sustained, what happens to knowledge under enclosure, and why that enclosure persists ungoverned. Epistemic sustainability is the capacity of a knowledge system to remain durable, plural, and transmissible across time without structural dependence on extractive, proprietary, or epistemically homogenising infrastructure, extending Scheman's (2012) norm from the ethics of inquiry to the political economy of knowledge infrastructure. Epistemic enclosure names the mechanism: the print-to-digital-to-AI trajectory, narrated as democratising, renders postcolonial knowledge traditions legible only on terms they did not set, through architectures optimised for English-language statistical patterns. Indian languages account for approximately 0.5 per cent of Common Crawl data, a major source corpus for language-model training; traditions including Nyaya, Mimamsa, and Ayurveda are rendered legible through patent classification, formal logic, and metadata standards external to their conditions of intelligibility. Double concealment names the ideological operation sustaining this enclosure: material infrastructural costs are externalised from green AI accounting, while the foreclosure of non-Western epistemic plurality is rendered invisible behind narratives of democratised access. 

The paper proposes three governance instruments: epistemic impact assessments for public AI infrastructure investment; a policy framework distinguishing compute from knowledge sovereignty; and multilateral mechanisms protecting the epistemic commons of postcolonial traditions in global AI regimes. As India approaches its 2047 centenary, the governance question its AI discourse has not yet asked is whether the knowledge it produces will remain answerable to India's plural epistemic traditions, or merely processed through infrastructures designed elsewhere.

articles.title: New Perspectives on Gender Identity and Fertility Ideals in Australia
articles.authors: Natalie Nitsche; Xioaxian Qiu; Ben Edwards; Daniela Grunow; Markus Hahn; Mary Lou Rasmussen
articles.abstract: Binary conceptualizations of gender are not only scientifically obsolete; they also may obscure important gender variation in fertility motivations. We offer a novel perspective on gender and its link with fertility ideals by conceptualizing gender identity as a multi-dimensional latent construct.
