We use measures on self-rated masculinity, femininity and gender identity importance from the 2024 Australian Social Survey International-ESS (AUSSI-ESS) to identify latent gender identity profiles and examine their association with fertility ideals among people aged 18-39. While the categorical gender measure showed no differences between cis-men and cis-women’s fertility ideals yet much lower fertility ideals among non-binary/trans people, multi-dimensional profiles revealed more nuanced patterns. Among childless respondents, the masculine profile had a significantly higher ideal number of children (1.52) than the feminine (1.17) and gender diverse (0.95) profiles. Notably, the gender diverse profile, combining moderate levels of self-assessed femininity, masculinity, and gender identity importance, was the largest among the childless, comprising 43 percent of the sample. This indicates stark variation in fertility ideals withing cis-gender groups, which remains masked by classical categorical gender measures. Hence, multi-dimensional gender conceptualizations appear to provide not only more inclusive but also more precise insights into contemporary fertility preferences.

articles.title: The Constituency for Personal Politicians: Social Embeddedness and Voter Behavior in Indonesia
articles.authors: Harry Janos Dienes; Burhanuddin Muhtadi; Hui Yuan Neo; Eitan Paul
articles.abstract: Do voters support personal intervention by politicians to facilitate access to public services? Does contingency – the defining characteristic of clientelism – matter? We conduct a survey experiment to test Indonesian voter reactions to three political service delivery strategies: impartial bureaucratic monitoring, personal intervention for all constituents, and clientelistic intervention for supporters only. Personal intervention is punished compared to programmatic monitoring, and contingency generates no further electoral costs than non-partisan personal intervention. Yet through a candidate survey, we find elected candidates make deals for access to services more often than unelected ones. To reconcile these findings, we show that social embeddedness moderates reactions. Voters with low social density and those who have approached politicians or bureaucrats for help find personal or clientelistic strategies as appealing as programmatic. These groups constitute a (minority) constituency for personal intervention as a legitimate electoral strategy. The results emphasize social relationships in voter reactions to clientelism.

articles.title: Beyond the Party: Campaign Visit Effects in Indonesia’s 2024 Election
articles.authors: Harry Janos Dienes; Jahen Fachrul Rezki; Burhanuddin Muhtadi; Afrimadona
articles.abstract: Evidence on campaign visits originates from established democracies, yet many democracies feature weak party attachments, personalism, and fluid coalitions that might strengthen effects. We combine a hand-collected, geocoded dataset of visits by Indonesia’s incumbent president with pooled data from 150 campaign surveys. Our data permit distinguishing effects across time and across types of electoral strategies. Comparing respondents near visit dates, we estimate a short 7pp increase in voting intention for the president’s chosen successor, driven by visibly distributing handouts or interacting with residents. These effects are transient: even in a case favourable to personalist persuasion, there is no impact after two weeks or on the final election result, for any type.

articles.title: Adjusting to the Other: Audiencing Through Gesture in Karnatak Vocal Lessons
articles.authors: Lara Pearson
articles.abstract: In addition to their pedagogic dimensions, music lessons are contexts for performing and audiencing. This article focuses on performance-audiency interactions in Karnatak vocal lessons in South India, exploring how teachers and students audience each other. Drawing on work from phenomenological and pragmatist traditions, I analyse ways that gesture, gaze and utterance contribute to teachers’ and students’ grip over their interactions, both with the other person and with the music performed. Through this analysis I develop the concept of audiency as an active and embodied ‘adjustment to the other’, and aim to further understanding of music as interaction.

articles.title: Futures of Terror Capitalism
articles.authors: Armando Garcia; Kevin Walby
articles.abstract: Abstract: Terror capitalism, as conceptualized by Byler (2022), fuses U.S. surveillance capitalism with the Chinese state’s social credit scoring, re-education, and coercive labor practices characteristic of authoritarian regimes. In this article, we argue that this assemblage now projects three geopolitical futures: a scaling up into a hemispheric “terror capital” race as an extension of what Besteman (2020) terms militarized global apartheid; a scaling down into domestic algorithmic and epistemic, bordering and carceral regimes; and a tempering through European regulatory friction. We focus on the first possible future, specifically the maturation of a new Monroe Doctrine, a 2026 “Trump Corollary” that shifts from an ostensibly defensive hemispheric posture to assertive, extractive interventionism. Analyzing the January 2026 U.S. intervention in Venezuela and the subsequent energy siege of Cuba, we demonstrate how the weaponization of resource scarcity and migration flows functions as a signature framework of mid‑twenty‑first‑century governing rationality. Our analysis foregrounds the entanglement of imperialism, state violence, and capital accumulation, or accumulation by immobilization, in the governance of global crisis.

articles.title: The Fear of Forgetting: The Reasons & Methods By Which Bhutanese-Nepali Refugees Work to Preserve Their Cultural Identities
articles.authors: Aryaa Rajouria
articles.abstract:
The Hindu, Nepali speaking Southern Bhutanese have always been seen as being dissimilar to the rest of the Buddhist, Dzongkha speaking population.  At the start of the 20th century, however, dissimilarity turned into discrimination. The Southern Bhutanese people with Nepali descent were given a choice. They could either absolutely disengage with their own culture and agree to acclimate to the Buddhist ways, or they were exterminated. A majority of the population decided to continue partake in their own culture, and were thus, violently expelled from the nation. 

As a result of an exclusionary sovereign who sought to create an ethnically united nation, the Southern Bhutanese fled the country. Since then, this population who identify themselves as the Bhutanese-Nepalese have migrated several times: first to refugee camps in Eastern Nepal, where they believed their ancestors once dwelled, or nearby locations in India and then they were scattered all over the world, particularly places like United States, Canada, and Australia. 

While the Bhutanese-Nepalese refugee population in Massachusetts has inhabited the area for almost a decade how, the members of the older female generation have yet to assimilate. Linguistic barriers and divergent lifestyles cause the Bhutanese Nepalese population to fold within their own. Based on a snowball-sampled focus group, I demonstrate that the women of the Bhutanese-Nepalese community preserve their distinct cultural identity through the practice of religion and by utilization of their language as a means by which to validate their survival after histories of multiple migrations and expulsion. By doing so, these women are creating a Bhutanese-Nepalese nation.

articles.title: Does Incivility Affect Message Persuasiveness in Citizens' Online Political Communication? Evidence from Japan
articles.authors: Kohei Nishi
articles.abstract: While some previous studies investigated the effect of incivility from political elites on persuasiveness of messages, the effect of incivility from ordinary citizens on message persuasiveness remains less explored. In the present study, I examined the effect of incivility from citizens on message persuasiveness in online political communication. I hypothesized that an uncivil political comment would be less persuasive than a civil one. I also proposed hypotheses focusing on how political interest and the status of agreement with a message might moderate the effect. I conducted a pre-registered online survey experiment with a Japanese sample. As a result, I did not find evidence that an uncivil political comment is, on average, less persuasive than a civil one. Meanwhile, I found that participants who had agreeing attitudes toward the presented comment before experimental treatment were more likely to be negatively affected by incivility than those who did not (only when covariates were not controlled). The results imply a possibility that exposure to an uncivil political comment from an in-group member may weaken pre-existing attitudes because it reduces trust in the in-group.

articles.title: Poverty and cardiovascular diseases: Individual and neighbourhood effects using a registry-based study in Czechia
articles.authors: Josef Bernard; Klára Benešová; Martin Bobák; Dagmar Dzurova; Klára Hulíková Tesárková; Lukáš Kahoun; Pavlína Netrdová
articles.abstract: The study investigated the relationship between poverty, place, and cardiovascular health in a Central and Eastern European country with a high burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD). We examined the effects of individual and neighbourhood poverty on CVD. We analysed data linked across several national registers covering 5.1 million working-age residents of Czechia (2019–2024), combining individual health and socioeconomic records with neighbourhood poverty measures. Individual poverty and neighbourhood poverty were assessed by receipt of subsistence-level poverty social benefits. The outcome was defined as CVD-related hospitalisation and/or mortality (ICD-10 I00–I99). Associations of CVD with individual and neighbourhood poverty were analysed using logistic regression models while accounting for residential sorting. Individual poverty was strongly associated with CVD-related hospitalisation and mortality, with individuals experiencing poverty exhibiting more than twice the odds of CVD. Living in a high-poverty neighbourhood was also associated with increased CVD risk, although the contextual effect was substantially smaller than the individual-level effect. The findings demonstrate that both individual and neighbourhood poverty independently shape cardiovascular health. While individual socioeconomic disadvantage is the dominant predictor of CVD risk, neighbourhood poverty exerts a smaller contextual influence. Incorporating place-based measures into health research can improve the identification of socially vulnerable populations and advance understanding of how local socioeconomic environments contribute to health inequalities.

articles.title: Unseen, Unheard, Undervalued: Relational Mechanisms of Gender Inequality in the Dutch IT Sector
articles.authors: Elise Jantine van der Mark
articles.abstract: Despite decades of policy progress, workplace gender equality in the Netherlands has stalled. Male-dominated sectors such as IT remain among the most unequal and exclusionary for women. Addressing these inequalities requires attention to women’s lived experiences, yet empirical research on Dutch women in IT remains strikingly limited. Drawing on feminist relational theory and the Gender@Work framework, this paper develops a relational diagnostic approach. It examines how gender inequality is (re)produced through everyday workplace interactions. The empirical basis consists of in-depth interviews (n=27) and three participatory group sessions (n=33). Adopting a participatory action research design, the study centers women's own accounts and collective analysis of their workplace experiences. The data reveal a dense web of interactions and relations involving colleagues, managers, clients, and institutional actors. Within these interactions, inequality is enacted through patterned relational practices rather than isolated incidents. Microaggressions, epistemic exclusion, and everyday interactional dynamics operate across contexts to contest women’s legitimacy, regulate their voice, and mark their embodied presence as deviant from the masculine norm. The analysis identifies seven recurring relational mechanisms through which gender inequality is systematically reproduced across interconnected domains. This extends Acker's concept of gendered organizations and offers a diagnostic framework with concrete entry points for organizational intervention.

articles.title: Police legitimacy in Bangladesh: a review of trust, accountability, and democratic governance
articles.authors: Ashfaq Ferdous; Sayed Osman Goni Rafat
articles.abstract: This study reviews and synthesises the literature on police legitimacy in Bangladesh. Drawing on 55 sources published between 1979 and 2026, it examines how legitimacy has been conceptualised, the factors that shape it, and the implications of recent accountability and reform debates. The findings show that police legitimacy in Bangladesh cannot be understood through procedural justice alone but is shaped by the interaction of citizen experiences, institutional performance, accountability arrangements, community engagement, and democratic governance. The literature identifies six interconnected themes: conceptualisations of legitimacy, trust and procedural justice, institutional sources of legitimacy, accountability deficits, community engagement, and democratic policing and reform. It also reveals a shift from concerns with trust and procedural fairness towards greater attention to accountability, democratic oversight, reform, and legitimacy restoration, particularly in the post-2024 context. The study develops a multi-level framework integrating interactional, institutional, and democratic dimensions of legitimacy and identifies priorities for future research.

articles.title: Does Incivility Influence Message Persuasiveness in Online Political Communication? Evidence from Japan
articles.authors: Kohei Nishi
articles.abstract: While some previous studies investigated the effect of incivility from political elites on message persuasiveness, the effect of incivility from ordinary citizens on message persuasiveness is less investigated. Thus, in the present study, I investigated the effect of incivility from citizens on message persuasiveness in online political communication. I hypothesized that an uncivil political comment is less persuasive than a civil one. I also proposed hypotheses about how political interest and the status of agreement with a message might moderate the effect. I conducted a pre-registered online survey experiment with a Japanese sample, in which participants were shown a randomly selected civil or uncivil political comment. As a result, I did not find evidence that an uncivil political comment is, on average, less persuasive than a civil one. Meanwhile, I found that participants who had agreeing attitudes toward the presented comment before experimental treatment were more likely to be negatively influenced by incivility than those who did not (only when covariates were not controlled). The results suggest a possibility that exposure to an uncivil political comment from an in-group member may weaken pre-existing attitudes because it reduces trust in the in-group or people want to avoid being seen as an associate of the person with rude manners.

articles.title: Plurality in transformative change: three co-created pathways toward nature-positive Europe(s)
articles.authors: Mara de Pater; Aniek Hebinck; Symke Nieboer; Anita Lazurko; Robbert Biesbroek; Laura Pereira; Elizabeth Díaz-General; Samia Baadj; Anna Chilton; Seweryn Krupnik
articles.abstract:
1.	The accelerating decline of biodiversity necessitates transformative change to protect nature and society, requiring innovative actions and governance strategies. This paper focuses on developing diverse transformative pathways for biodiversity in Europe and advancing methodologies for co-creating these pathways to inform such actions and governance strategies in a transformative and anticipatory manner.
2.	Three distinct pathways for a nature-positive Europe from 2024 to 2050 were co-created with 23 participants during a 2.5-day workshop, through backcasting and by using the Nature Futures Framework. Post-workshop interviews with nine participants helped map their understanding of transformative change and its connection to the pathways. The pathways and interviews were then analysed to understand the main patterns of change in the pathways.
3.	The analysis identifies distinct patterns of transformative change, each shaped by participants’ views on how change might unfold over time, as reflected in pathway actions and milestones. The first pathway, called Dòigh Nàdair, centres on the institutionalisation of biocultural principles, community stewardship, and redistribution toward rural economies, with early emphasis on phasing out unsustainable practices, shifting societal norms through education, and later embedding polycentric and watershed-based governance. The second, NaturAll, focuses on sufficiency and ecological limits, combining restrictive regulation with participatory programmes, progressive caps and land reallocation, and staged policy development from pilots to broader implementation. The third, Return to Nature, emphasises strengthened governmental mandates, expert consultation, and the mainstreaming of climate and biodiversity goals through innovation and coordinated governance, with crises reinforcing support for reform. 
4.	The pathways demonstrate how diverse patterns and understandings of transformative change can result in a range of desired nature-positive futures, effectively turning concepts of transformative change into practical actions. The techniques employed in creating these pathways play a crucial role in shaping the results, necessitating intentional design that aligns with specific objectives. This highlights the importance of developing plural pathways to investigate multiple potential nature-positive futures, all while preserving a strong sense of ambition and urgency for transformative action.

articles.title: Attrition Bias in AI-Administered Interviews
articles.authors: Mikkel Stahlschmidt; Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus; Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Who finishes an AI-administered interview, and how does that group differ from who finishes a standard survey? We report a pre-registered four-arm randomized experiment (N = 1,591) assigning Danish online-panel adults to a standardized survey, a standardized chat, an adaptive AI chat, and an extended adaptive AI chat, all covering same substantive content. Completion falls monotonically from 91.8% to 66.7% across arms. The chat interface drives most of the gap (a 14.6 percentage-point drop), limited adaptive probing adds almost nothing (2.3 percentage-point), and extended probing leads to exhaustion and attrition (8.2 percentage-point). Dropout is socially selective: in the most demanding arm, respondents aged 18 to 34 are more likely to complete than those aged 56 and older, and completers are more educated and more likely to use a computer rather than a smartphone. AI-interview samples are therefore younger, more educated, and more desktop-oriented, with direct consequences for inference of results.

articles.title: Paz Total? How Ceasefires Backfire
articles.authors: Juan F. Vargas; Daniel Mejia; Andrés F. Rivera
articles.abstract: Ceasefires are often designed to reduce violence while facilitating peace negotiations or humanitarian access. But poorly designed truces can backfire. This paper examines the 2023 ceasefires decreed by Colombia’s government with several organized criminal groups simultaneously under the Paz Total (Total Peace) policy. Using difference-in-differences on a municipality-month panel, we find that while more visible and salient forms of violence such as homicides, terrorist attacks and massacres were unaffected, less visible forms of violence against civilians, such as extortion, forced recruitment of minors, and threats, increased substantially in municipalities with ceasefire group presence. These patterns are consistent with strategic substitution: armed groups shifted from more visible to less visible forms of violence when political constraints changed. We formalize this mechanism in a structural model of strategic violence allocation, calibrate its parameters to the reduced-form estimates, and simulate policy counterfactuals. The calibration implies that roughly a 50% increase in the detectability of less visible forms of violence, through independent verification missions or community reporting systems, would be needed to fully offset the ceasefire’s perverse effects, restoring total violence to approximately its pre-ceasefire level. Our findings highlight the unintended consequences of inadequately designed ceasefire agreements and underscore the need for credible monitoring and enforcement mechanisms.

articles.title: A Guiding Framework for Backdated Nutrient Stock Reconstruction and Valuation in Residual Fertility Accounting
articles.authors: Harrison Coker; Madelynn M. Fisher; Jason P. Sardella
articles.abstract: Tax-oriented materials on residual or excess soil fertility deductions indicate demand for methods that document the presence, extent, attribution, and exhaustion of acquired nutrient stocks over time. The objective of this protocol is to outline a standardized residual fertility accounting protocol for use in tax-position purposes. The protocol defines residual fertility as the plant-available nutrient stock within a specified management depth at acquisition, measured with accepted soil-test methods in a robust spatial design, reconstructed by a backdated nutrient mass balance, and translated to economic value by transparent nutrient price series. The backdating framework incorporates four modules: (1) post-acquisition nutrient additions, (2) nutrient export in products, (3) erosion-related losses, and (4) leaching and volatilization. The protocol recommends explicit reporting of sampling design, utilization of representative property means, historical management evidence tiers, and uncertainty analysis. The protocol provides a standardized framework for a field in which practice currently exceeds peer-reviewed methodology.

articles.title: Occupational Safety and Health Management in Very Small Enterprises: A Scoping Review Protocol
articles.authors: Marion Poirier; Jessica Dubé; Anouk Aubert-Simard; Benedicte Nauche; Caroline Jolly
articles.abstract: Very small enterprises (VSEs), defined as organizations with 1 to 19 employees, represent 88.4% of Canadian businesses. Despite their economic weight, their occupational safety and health (OSH) practices remain poorly documented, and the literature focuses mainly on larger enterprises. This scoping review aims to identify and map OSH activities in VSEs across OECD countries, including prevention practices, implementation strategies, and organizational factors, in a context where limited material, financial, and human resources often pose challenges for OSH management. Guided by the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the JBI approach, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Scopus will be systematically searched for English- or French-language publications from 2014 to 2024. The search strategies will be developed by a specialized librarian (BN) and will be described in detail in the supplementary material 1. Records will be independently screened by two reviewers (ergonomists AAS and MP), and data will be extracted by the full research team (AAS, MP, CJ, and JD) using a structured charting form. Extracted information will include study characteristics; OSH topics (e.g., workplace safety, injury or accident prevention, risk assessment, training and information, health promotion); the person responsible (e.g., worker, owner-manager, or external stakeholder); and reported facilitators and barriers to integrating these OSH strategies. Descriptive mapping and thematic synthesis will be conducted, with study management supported by Covidence® and thematic charting supported by NVivo 15®. Findings will be disseminated through submission to the interdisciplinary journal WORK: A Journal of Prevention, Assessment & Rehabilitation and through presentations at scientific and professional events, in support of a broader six-project research program on OSH management in Québec VSEs (Dubé et al., 2024). By highlighting OSH strategies used by VSE owner-managers and workers, this scoping review will support researchers, practitioners, and policy stakeholders seeking feasible, context-sensitive approaches to improve OSH in micro-enterprises and very small businesses.

articles.title: Economic Segregation, Political Participation, and Social Capital
articles.authors: Selene Campion; Andreas Wiedemann
articles.abstract: Rising economic inequality has reshaped residential patterns across rich democracies, yet the political consequences of economic segregation remain poorly understood. We argue that the spatial configuration of inequality amplifies class-based disparities in participation by reinforcing socio-economic (dis-)advantage and weakening cross-class networks. Combining fine-grained, grid-based measures of segregation with local election results from German municipalities between 2005 and 2021, we show, using instrumental-variables analyses, that turnout is lower in segregated places. Original survey data reveal that segregation widens turnout gaps by disproportionately demobilizing low-income voters. However, these effects depend on local social capital: using administrative records of all civic associations, we show that turnout in segregated places declines where associations are scarce but increases where dense community and welfare organizations bridge economic divides and alleviate material constraints. This suggests that the spatial structure of inequality and the strength of civic associations shape political inequality beyond individual socio-economic status.

articles.title: Carry-over effects in the within-subject spectator task
articles.authors: Linda Dezső; Antal Ertl; Valeriia Chukaeva; Gergely Hajdu
articles.abstract: The spectator task elicits third parties’ inequality acceptance, allowing researchers to estimate population distributions of fairness-preference types. In its within-subject form, spectators make two subsequent choices in situations involving merit- and luck-based inequalities with randomized order. We document a carry-over effect: redistribution is lower in the second choice, and inferred fairness-type distributions vary with choice order. We cannot determine whether this pattern is driven by a psychological mechanism active during repeated choices or a contrast between inequality causes. Either interpretation implies a violation of causal transience and calls for caution when using this design.

articles.title: An ESCO-Based Skill-Gap Detection Framework for SMEs: A Design Science Prototype of an Intelligent Learning Management System
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Nicola Magaletti; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta
articles.abstract: The growing misalignment between workforce competences and the skill requirements of digitally evolving occupations is a critical barrier to SME competitiveness in the Industry 4.0 and 5.0 transitions. This study develops and demonstrates, through a working prototype, an ESCO-aligned analytical framework for skill-gap detection and adaptive reskilling, produced within the LUCE (LUtech Campus Ecosystem) project. Its contribution is theoretical, methodological, and technological rather than purely applicative. Drawing on human capital theory, the knowledge-based view of the firm, and skill-biased technical change, it conceptualizes reskilling as the relaxation of a firm-level human-capital–technology complementarity constraint, using ESCO to render this constraint observable and commensurable across firms. Methodologically, it defines the skill gap as a standardized, ontology-grounded measure; technologically, it integrates functions usually kept separate — performance analytics, skill assessment, and learning provision — into a single pipeline, instantiated as a proof-of-concept Intelligent Learning Management System. Workforce competences are extracted from anonymized employee CVs via a deterministic, rule-based Natural Language Processing procedure, mapped to ESCO preferred labels, alternative labels, and concept URIs, and linked to occupational requirements through occupation–skill relations. A Skill Gap Indicator, defined as the complement of evidenced ESCO competence coverage, yields a mean of 0.956, interpreted as a conservative upper-bound estimate rather than a literal measure of absent competences. The prototype then translates detected gaps into targeted training recommendations. As a research prototype, the system is validated along its technical and analytical dimensions rather than for training effectiveness; the relationship between gap closure and firm performance is advanced as a proposition for future longitudinal evaluation.

articles.title: Angel Versus Devil: Ethical and Unethical Leadership Case Study Comparison
articles.authors: JianYuan Chen; Hao Puyan
articles.abstract:
Leadership significantly influences organizational performance, ethical governance, and sustainable development. This study compares two contrasting historical leaders, Charles Ponzi and Robert Owen, to examine the impacts of unethical and ethical leadership on corporate social responsibility (CSR) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Using a comparative case study approach based on historical evidence and business ethics literature, the research analyzes their leadership styles, decision-making processes, and long-term social consequences.
The findings indicate that Ponzi's deceptive and fraudulent leadership generated short-term financial gains but ultimately destroyed stakeholder trust, caused substantial economic losses, and undermined sustainable development. In contrast, Owen's servant and ethical leadership promoted employee welfare, education, social equity, and responsible management, demonstrating that ethical leadership can create lasting organizational and societal value. The study further discusses how ethical decision-making, transparency, and corporate governance can reduce unethical behavior and strengthen CSR practices.
This research concludes that although unethical leadership may produce temporary success, ethical leadership provides stronger foundations for organizational sustainability, stakeholder confidence, and long-term competitive advantage. The findings offer practical implications for business leaders, policymakers, and management educators seeking to promote responsible leadership and sustainable organizational development.

articles.title: Opera decolonized - Listening to Afghan Women’s Voices
articles.authors: Kasia Głowicka
articles.abstract:
Opera is a form where music, staging, dramaturgy, costume, and space are co-
equal — a total sensory experience that demands full presence from its
audience. This paper investigates whether that formal quality can be turned
against opera's own colonial tendencies. Working within The Airport Society
collective, I examine how the opera-installation Unknown, I Live With You
(2018), setting clandestine writings by Afghan women, transforms opera's
European form into a respectful artistic space for non-European voices. I
argue that interlocking formal decisions together refuse the patronizing
frameworks that historically position non-European subjects as exotic victims
requiring Western salvation. The non-hierarchical structure of the work
extends to the collective process that produced it: the same democratic
principle governing our artistic decisions shapes what the audience
experiences. The result is cross-cultural listening that treats Afghan women's
socio-political reflections with intellectual gravity rather than humanitarian
condescension.

articles.title: El jurista que interpreta a la máquina: despachos de inteligencia artificial, monopolio de la postulación y acceso a la justicia a propósito del caso Garfield AI (Reino Unido)
articles.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles.abstract: n mayo de 2026, Garfield AI —el primer despacho de servicios jurídicos del Reino Unido autorizado y regulado por la Solicitors Regulation Authority para operar principalmente mediante inteligencia artificial— obtuvo, ante el Tribunal del Condado de Wandsworth, la primera victoria de un «despacho de IA» en un juicio contradictorio frente a una parte asistida por abogados tradicionales. Este trabajo sostiene que el dato relevante no es la sustitución del abogado por una máquina, sino la inversión funcional de roles: la IA produce los documentos y el jurista deviene intérprete y responsable de lo generado. A partir del caso se examina el modelo regulatorio británico (autorizar a la firma, no a la máquina), se lo contrasta con la matriz estadounidense (Regla 5.4 del Modelo ABA, doctrina del ejercicio no autorizado del Derecho y sandboxes de Utah y Arizona) y europea (Reglamento (UE) 2024/1689 y Carta Ética de la CEPEJ), y se evalúa su trasladabilidad al ordenamiento chileno. Se concluye que el obstáculo chileno no reside en la propiedad de la firma —la colegiatura es voluntaria desde 1981 y no rige una prohibición equivalente a la Regla 5.4— sino en el monopolio personal de la postulación (Ley N° 18.120, arts. 1 y 2), reforzado por sanción penal (art. 3) y por el carácter intuitu personae del título de abogado (arts. 521 y 527 del Código Orgánico de Tribunales). La ficción de la «firma-IA» no es trasplantable; sí lo es, en cambio, su función legítima: la inteligencia artificial como herramienta de preparación bajo patrocinio, firma y responsabilidad de un abogado habilitado. https://zenodo.org/records/20848233

articles.title: Family Context, Directed and Random Exploration Profiles, and Child Socioemotional Functioning
articles.authors: Zhi Li; Yuanzhe Li; Patrick Davies; Melissa Sturge-Apple
articles.abstract: Guided by the evolutionary developmental perspective, this multi-method, longitudinal study seeks to examine “hyperparameters” that organize young children’s learning. In particular, we adopt computational modeling and a person-centered approach to characterize children’s exploration-exploitation profiles during a reward-probability task. We also explored the family socioeconomic precursors and child psychological sequelae of the profiles. Participants were 243 families with a preschooler (Mean age=4.60 years, 56% girls) from diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds (46% Black, 19% Latinx). Family socioeconomic risks were measured at wave one, and exploration-exploitation and socioemotional functioning were assessed two years later via a reward probability task and teacher-report, respectively. Person-centered approach revealed three exploration-exploitation profiles, reflecting (a) a high-random exploration, (b) a high-directed exploration, and (c) a balanced exploration-exploitation profile. Greater family socioeconomic risk was linked to an elevated likelihood of membership in the high-random-exploration profile (e.g., Z = -2.37). In turn, the high-random-exploration profile exhibited the highest attention problems and greater externalizing problems. Findings have critical implications for understanding the processes through which children adapt to adverse family contexts.

articles.title: El gato de Schrödinger en el Tribunal Supremo:  la  irregularidad regular del solicitante de asilo
articles.authors: MOBILE - Center of Excellence for Global Mobility Law; Lucía López Zurita
articles.abstract:
¿Puede un solicitante de asilo estar a la vez en situación regular, que no le permite solicitar 
una residencia excepcional por arraigo, e irregular, de modo que su permanencia en el país sea 
meramente tolerada, pese a venir exigida por el derecho europeo? Si las Directivas de asilo no han 
sido transpuestas en derecho nacional, ¿qué papel corresponde al Tribunal Supremo al aplicarlas? Y, 
por último, ¿cuál es la influencia de la jurisprudencia del Tribunal Supremo en las reformas 
legislativas posteriores? Este artículo da respuesta a estas preguntas a través del análisis de la 
jurisprudencia del Supremo sobre el estatus jurídico de los demandantes de asilo pendientes de 
resolución definitiva.

articles.title: A Practice-Oriented Approach to (De)Legitimation:  Materiality, Embodied Practices, and Normativity
articles.authors: MOBILE - Center of Excellence for Global Mobility Law; Nora Stappert; Frank Gadinger
articles.abstract:
This forum proposes a practice-oriented approach to (de)legitimation processes in world politics. 
Drawing on international practice theory and visual IR, among other fields, our approach offers an 
important extension of existing literature on (de)legitimation that mostly concentrates on discursive 
(de)legitimation. Instead, this forum focuses on a broader variety of practices of (de)legitimation, 
such as bodily gestures and visual (de)legitimation practices, including as communicated via (social) 
media. The forum’s six contributions demonstrate the significance and conceptual promise of our 
approach by showcasing various conceptual entry points and empirical illustrations. Matthias Ecker
Ehrhardt analyzes the everyday legitimation practices of international organization officials acting as 
the “personal face” of institutional processes on social media. Anna Geis examines the Taliban’s 
symbolic and embodied practices of self-legitimation during the Doha negotiations with the United 
States in 2019–2020. Subsequently, Stanislav Budnitsky conceptualizes the reoccurring practice of 
verbally and physically assaulting foreign experts on Russian televised political talk shows as 
embodied legitimation practices of Russia’s anti-Western geopolitical agenda. David Shim and 
Laurenz Krumbacher draw attention to the everyday, visualized legitimation practices of climate 
activists on TikTok, emphasizing their performative dimension. Frank Gadinger turns to Volodymyr 
Zelenskyy’s social media-oriented public performances in parliaments around the world. Nora 
Stappert and Siddharth Tripathi conclude the forum with a discussion of limitations, remaining 
challenges, and future research avenues, including using decolonial and postcolonial approaches. 
Combined, our forum opens an avenue for future research that considers existing and new forms of 
(de)legitimation in global affairs through the lens of practice while emphasizing the crucial role of 
legitimacy and normativity in international practices.

articles.title: Boomers vs. Zoomers? Age Stereotypes and Fairness Evaluations in the Workplace
articles.authors: Marcel Knobloch; Sophia Hunger; Lena Hipp
articles.abstract: According to public media debates, today's workplaces are characterized by generational tensions, citing stereotypes such as "lazy Gen Z" and "irresponsible Boomers.” Whether these perceived generational tensions manifest in age-based stereotypes and differential evaluations in workplace settings, however, remains an open question. To address this question, we draw on unique survey data from Germany (N = 2,229) to provide a nuanced exploration of cohort-specific stereotypes and their impact on fairness evaluations of workplace behaviors. Building on theories of status characteristics and social identity, we examine how age shapes perceptions, stereotypes, attitudes, and discriminatory behaviors. First, we conducted a WikiSurvey to explore common stereotypes about younger and older individuals, revealing the positive and negative perceptions respondents hold toward both their own and other age groups. Second, we replicate survey questions from the European Social Survey on ageism with the same respondents. We find that while younger people view both their peers and older individuals positively, older people tend to favor their own age group. Third, we conducted a survey experiment to assess the causal effect of age on evaluations of workplace behaviors and find that older respondents evaluate the behaviors of potential older co-workers as fairer than the exact same behaviors of younger co-workers. There is, however, no statistically significant difference between younger respondents’ views on the same behavior for older and younger col-leagues. Taken together, our findings provide evidence for age-based in-group favoritism, in particular among older people, which may have significant consequences for collaboration, productivity, and organizational cohesion.

articles.title: ROI and the Misclassification of Criminal Justice Education Programs: How Accountability Metrics Shape Public Universities and the Evaluation of CJ Education
articles.authors: Sandra L. Trappen
articles.abstract: Criminal Justice (CJ) education programs at public universities are increasingly evaluated through state level ROI frameworks that tie program value to short term earnings and workforce alignment. This article shows how these models, now embedded in many funding and accountability regimes, tend to misclassify CJ education programs. Descriptive data from the National Center for O*NET Development, BLS, College Scorecard, and state salary databases reveal three key structural mismatches: most CJ occupations do not require a bachelor’s degree; public sector wage structures depress early career earnings; and ROI classifications shift with occupational and temporal definitions. As a result, ROI models capture labor market composition and state funding priorities rather than program value, obscuring CJ’s civic and community roles.

articles.title: Gobernanza deliberativa y salud pública
articles.authors: Luis Fernando Gómez
articles.abstract: Este ensayo aborda los conceptos básicos de gobernanza deliberativa aplicada a la salud pública. Se plantea que los procesos de gobernanza son de doble filo. Por una parte, brindan la oportunidad de ampliar la participación ciudadana en asuntos públicos, como es el caso de los Consejos de Participación en Salud en Brasil. Otros enfoques de gobernanza propenden por un Estado mínimo que favorece alianzas público-privadas entre agencias gubernamentales e industrias como el tabaco, alcohol y comestibles ultraprocesados, en detrimento de la salud pública. Se plantea que la gobernanza deliberativa ofrece una perspectiva que concilia la urgencia de tomar acciones en asuntos relacionados con la salud pública con el imperativo de reconocer a la ciudadanía como autora de sus propias normas.

articles.title: A HISTÓRIA ECONÔMICA NO BRASIL
articles.authors: Thales Zamberlan Pereira
articles.abstract: Este artigo analisa aproximadamente 50 mil teses e dissertações defendidas em departamentos de história e economia ao longo das últimas quatro décadas, com o objetivo de mapear a evolução da história econômica no Brasil e oferecer aos interessados um guia para o desenvolvimento da área. Antes da análise empírica, centrada no período 1980-2022, apresento um panorama histórico que cobre desde o surgimento dos estudos de caráter ensaístico, predominantes até a década de 1950, até o amadurecimento da produção acadêmica. Esse processo teve início na década de 1960, com a contribuição dos “brasilianistas”, e consolidou-se a partir dos anos 1980, quando a expansão dos programas de pós-graduação em diferentes regiões do país firmou a pesquisa monográfica e especializada como padrão dominante da disciplina.

articles.title: The Measure Makes the Finding: How measurement, design, and framing shape what we conclude about race, democracy, and punishment in the U.S. states
articles.authors: Miura Meng
articles.abstract: What we conclude about inequality depends not only on the data but on the choices we make in handling them, a point pressed for years under banners like data feminism and QuantCrit and formalized in multiverse analysis. This paper makes it concrete. It takes one high-stakes question, race, democracy, and punishment across the U.S. states, and carries it through four ordinary analytic choices: which measure of inequality to report, whether to compare states or follow each over time, how many groups to read into the data, and whether to judge a reform by its text or its effect. The answer moves at every step, and at the first it flips outright. One of these reversals travels well beyond the case: the Black/White imprisonment ratio improves with democracy only because the white rate falls, not because Black imprisonment does, so a widely used equity metric can move for reasons that have nothing to do with how Black people are treated. The deeper point is that the competing measures are not separate analyses but one model: a joint Bayesian multilevel model of the underlying imprisonment rates, in which they reappear as contrasts of a single posterior, and the sign reversal is reported as a probability rather than a row of figures. Methods include multilevel models, group-based trajectory modeling, synthetic control, and Bayesian model expansion.

articles.title: Do voters want (and reward) stricter political finance regulation? Evidence from South Africa.
articles.authors: Sarah Brierley; Daniel de Kadt
articles.abstract: Efforts to reduce political corruption often focus on stricter regulation of, and enhanced transparency about, political finance. Do voters favor such reforms, and do they reward (and punish) parties that enact (retrench) them? We examine these questions in South Africa, where the ruling African National Congress (ANC) introduced — and later effectively reversed— the Political Party Funding Act (PPFA), which de-anonymized donors and capped contributions. Using a nationally representative survey (N = 1800) with embedded experiments, we measure voter support for such regulations and test how information about the reform and its reversal shapes voter preferences. Although respondents generally express support for tighter regulations, they do not become more favorable toward the ANC after learning about the PPFA. Information about the reversal decreases declared ANC vote intention by around 5 percentage points. Auxiliary tests suggest that voters' doubts about the enforceability of the Act may explain the limited positive updating.

articles.title: The Red Queen at the Grassroots: The Co-Evolution of Cadre Resistance and  Regime Control
articles.authors: Xuanyuan Li
articles.abstract:
Why do Chinese grassroots cadres sometimes voluntarily report their own 
disciplinary violations, triggering investigations that suspend their impossible policy 
tasks? And what happens when the disciplinary system learns to strike back? Drawing 
on 32 in-depth interviews with current and former cadres in S City, H Province, 
combined with official statistics and policy documents (2020–2026), this paper 
documents an emerging phenomenon:"cadre self-informing",and traces its evolution 
from a rational risk-avoidance strategy to a failing one.
Self-informing becomes rational under a triple condition: fiscal depletion 
(local self-sufficiency rate below 35%), incentive inversion (the penalty for 
"incompetence" outweighs that for "corruption"), and the collapse of social trust. 
Facing zero-budget demolition tasks and catastrophic sanctions for failure, cadres 
strategically exploit a procedural rigidity,that every disciplinary report must be 
investigated,to pause the implementation clock and seek refuge in a bounded, 
predictable investigation rather than an unbounded, career-ending charge of 
incompetence.
Yet the system does not remain inert. Through longitudinal tracking of a key 
case,a cadre whose self-informing strategy survived a traditional investigation but 
unraveled spectacularly under an AI-enhanced one,this paper reveals that the 
disciplinary apparatus is itself a learning entity. AI-driven tools compressed 
investigation timelines, shattered the informational opacity "battle-tested" cadres had 
relied upon, and fundamentally recalibrated the risk calculus of self-informing.
Drawing on the Red Queen effect, this paper reconceptualizes the "execution 
limit" of China's pressure-based system not as a static boundary, but as a moving front 
in an ongoing arms race between agents and the institutions that discipline them. The 
findings advance institutional gap theory beyond state-society contention into internal 
regime-agent dynamics, and identify a "high-pressure trap" in adaptive 
authoritarianism: over-mobilization drains the very resources and trust that 
adaptability requires, generating the evasion it seeks to extinguish.

articles.title: Evaluating Nonuniform Dependability Across Response Conditions: A Conditional Generalizability Framework Illustrated in Automated Essay Scoring
articles.authors: Yi Gui
articles.abstract: Aggregate reliability and dependability estimates can obscure heterogeneity in measurement-design burden across response conditions; when this occurs, a single G- or D-study may mischaracterize the adequacy of a design for particular strata. This study introduces a conditional generalizability framework with three components. First, automated scoring configurations—the encoder architectures and scoring-head families admissible within a fixed development pipeline—are conceptualized as a universe of admissible measurement conditions rather than as incidental modeling choices. Second, analytical D-study projections are compared with empirical configuration sweeps over a finite scoring pool, yielding two estimands of design adequacy whose agreement or divergence diagnoses the realized configuration universe. Third, G- and D-study evidence is conditioned on entropy-defined response strata, treating entropy as an operational stratification variable, not as a construct claim about writing quality, so that both the aggregate and condition-specific design burden can be evaluated. Whereas recent extensions of generalizability theory have addressed AI-generated item variants on the response side, the present framework addresses an analogous scoring-side problem: AI-mediated scoring configurations. The framework is demonstrated using automated essay scoring of timed L2 writing tasks. The realized scoring design was dependable in aggregate (Φ ≈ .76 for the person × task × configuration design). Re-estimated at the essay level within entropy strata, dependability was uniformly high but declined modestly and robustly across strata (Φ = .88, .87, .84)—a small gradient that nonetheless implied different decision-study requirements, with the highest-entropy stratum needing more crossed scoring conditions to reach a given dependability target. Empirical configuration sweeps further indicate whether analytical minimum-design recommendations are attainable within the available scoring pool. The framework provides a portable workflow for evaluating nonuniform dependability whenever multiple scoring, rating, or observation configurations are available.

articles.title: From Plan to Pram: Type of Partnership in the Formation and Realisation of Fertility Intentions in Czechia
articles.authors: Eva Waldaufová
articles.abstract: Partnership forms in Europe have diversified: cohabitation encompasses unions that range from steps towards, to long-term alternatives to, marriage. Yet it remains unclear whether these distinctions shape solely the formation of short-term fertility intentions or also their realisation as births. Research into the significance of cohabitation has examined how intentions form without considering their translation into behaviour, whereas research into the intention–realisation gap has addressed cohabitation as a single, undifferentiated category. Employing data from two panel rounds of the Czech Generations and Gender Survey, each comprising a baseline and three-year follow-up (round 1: 2005 and 2008; round 2: 2020–2022 and 2025), binary and multinomial logistic regression was applied to examine whether the importance of partnership type differed at these two stages for women and men aged 18–44 in coresidential partnerships. The study distinguished married individuals, cohabitants who intended to marry and those without such intentions. Partnership type strongly differentiates the formation of fertility intentions: cohabitants who intend to marry are most likely to plan a child, whereas those without marriage intentions are substantially less likely to do so. These differences appeared to narrow over time (albeit marginally), in line with the normalisation of cohabitation. In contrast, no evidence was found that the legal or intentional character of the union is independently associated with realisation, once parity and intention certainty were accounted for. Overall, partnership type structures selection into fertility intentions, whereas their realisation appears to depend more on life-course position and motivational commitment than on institutional form.

articles.title: Systemic motonormativity
articles.authors: Jakub Sliacan; Matej Cibik
articles.abstract:
In contemporary societies, car-based transportation solutions have persistently held a strong position, being treated as the natural, even paramount form of mobility.  Our focus is on the recent addition to the study of this phenomenon, "motonormativity". Motonormativity aims to identify the specifically normative element at play: Why is automobility receiving a seemingly preferential treatment? Why do cars get such a high status in public spaces? To this end, Ian Walker and co-authors defined motonormativity as a "cultural inability to think objectively and dispassionately due to largely unconscious assumptions about how travel is", and attempted to establish its presence experimentally. We argue that, while the concept is valuable, Walker's (et al.) approach invites reassessment.

The first part of the paper spells out concerns with the current understanding of motonormativity. First, the "bias" take on motonormativity stipulates an "unbiased" baseline of judgement as a vantage point, which is problematic. Second, the definitions put forward are individualistic (as opposed to systemic). The second part of the paper presents a more comprehensive take on motonormativity as a hierarchy entrenched in the system, thereby positioning it as a system-level phenomenon that can be understood outside of the constraints of individual beliefs and actions.

articles.title: Language Development: Input, Multilingualism, and the Literacy Environment - A Blue Blocks Montessori School Home Observation Study, Hyderabad
articles.authors: Pavan Goyal; Sreemoyee Chakraborty; Raunak Sharma
articles.abstract: The present study investigates the home language environment of 99 children from Blue Blocks Montessori School, Hyderabad, for the period January-February 2026, focusing on three interrelated areas of interest: (i) amount and quality of adults’ linguistic input, (ii) type of the multilingual environment, and (iii) nature of home literacy environment. Based on the Montessori principle of the sensitive period for language (Montessori, 1949; Montessori, 1946) and recent research concerning language learning, bilingualism and early literacy (Hart & Risley, 1995; Cummins, 2000; Neuman & Dickinson, 2001), we analysed parental reports on story time and song singing, narrations of activities, conversation richness, and the variety and distribution of sources of input and information within a multilingual context, as well as reading practices and presence of books. Key findings include: a majority of children receive more than one hour of extended adult narrative daily; 88% live in multilingual households; mother is the primary language-input source in 43% of families; structured one-person-one-language practice is rarely maintained; mealtime conversation is predominantly child-led; and home literacy environments are moderately rich but with significant variability in book quantity and dedicated reading infrastructure. Parent reflective data illuminate a community in active, joyful language development. Implications for Montessori language pedagogy and home-school language partnership are discussed.

articles.title: Learning interdependence: youth arts as relational skills in Singapore
articles.authors: Rimi Parvin Khan
articles.abstract: This article examines how arts-based co-curricular activities (CCAs) in Singaporean higher education navigate the tension between state pragmatism and student experience. Situated within the SkillsFuture framework and a meritocratic ethos that instrumentalises education for economic productivity, arts programmes can be viewed as sites for acquiring ‘21st-century skills’. Drawing on qualitative research with university students involved in a range of arts CCAs this study explores the relationship between official discourses of individual skill accumulation and students' subjective accounts of these skills. While students acknowledge acquiring transferable competencies, their narratives highlight a distinct process of learning and working through interdependence. Rather than fostering individualised self-optimisation, arts CCAs become spaces where young people collaboratively negotiate cultural difference, adapt to diverse perspectives, and build relational capacity. The findings suggest that while students embody the contradictory pressures of neoliberal governance – balancing anxieties about career viability with a desire for ‘fun’ – the arts cultivate a critical, reflexive intersubjectivity. This embodied experience of interdependence offers a complex, collective response to diversity that challenges the atomised logic of labour market agendas, and highlights the need for accreditation frameworks that acknowledge students’ experiences and values.

articles.title: Enabling Sustainability Transitions in the Semiconductor Domain: Designing a Transition Practice–Education Cycle
articles.authors: Hiromi Kimoto; Maoko Fujisaki; Keito Inoue; Norio Kamitsubo; Kohei Saito; Sota Takagi; Takumi Ohashi
articles.abstract: Semiconductors are enabling technologies whose innovation is largely governed by technical roadmaps, leaving limited infrastructure for the normative deliberation and capability-building required for sustainability transitions. This paper asks how transition agenda formation can be connected to university-based education and project formation in the semiconductor sector. Drawing on Transition Design and Transition Management, we conceptualize the Transition Practice–Education Cycle (TPEC), a process framework that iteratively links transition agenda formation with industry and domain frontrunners, university-based Transition Design education, and project formation with committed stakeholders. Using Research through Design, we report an initial TPEC implementation at Institute of Science Tokyo in the semiconductor domain. The analysis identifies two translation functions absent from the initial design: Agenda-to-Education Translation and Project Translation and Validation. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a revised TPEC framework that embeds both as explicit design functions. The study also suggests Transition-oriented Semiconductor Capability as a potential educational goal for enabling technology sectors.

articles.title: Electoral systems shape the entry and entrenchment of extremist parties
articles.authors: Chanuwas Aswamenakul; Tyler Marghetis; Brad L. LeVeck; Paul E. Smaldino
articles.abstract: Representative democracies aspire to represent voters’ viewpoints through their elected officials. At the same time, they may try to minimize extremist viewpoints that can destabilize democracy itself. Here we show that electoral systems navigate this tension by trading off between two vulnerabilities: extremist entry and extremist entrenchment. Using computational models, we investigate how electoral systems respond to the emergence of ideological extremism arising either through the introduction of a new party or through the gradual radicalization of an established party. Systems that more accurately represent public opinion are more permissive to new parties, including extremist ones. Conversely, systems that suppress extremist entry can also protect incumbent parties as they drift toward increasingly extreme and unrepresentative positions. Electoral systems therefore differ not only in how well they represent voters or how many parties they sustain, but in the vulnerabilities they create: institutional openness increases the risk of extremist entry, while institutional inertia increases the risk of extremist entrenchment. Democracies thus face a fundamental design challenge: The same institutional features that protect a democracy from one extremist risk also expose it to another.

articles.title: Small Town, Big Overhead: Rural–Urban Differences in Administrative Cost per Student
articles.authors: Kallen Zhou
articles.abstract: Current literature on rural higher education institutions (HEIs) acknowledges the role they play in their communities, providing post-secondary education access and contributions to their local economies. Additionally, administrative bloat has been commonly defined as the increase in non-instructional spending. However, these analyses rarely considered how rurality can affect administrative bloat. Applying economic theories such as Resource Dependency Theory and diseconomies of scale, this study pairs a theoretical framework with quantitative analyses to investigate whether rural HEIs face larger growth in their administrative spending compared to their urban counterparts. Using IPEDS panel data (2006–2023), inflation-adjusted administrative spending per student, and a rural/urban classification based on IPEDS locale codes, this study combines descriptive comparisons, Welch’s unequal-variance t-tests, and a comparative interrupted time series design around the year 2011, a major federal compliance inflection point for higher education. The results indicate a statistically significant post-2011 rural-relative slope increase of approximately $174 per student per year in administrative spending compared to urban institutions (p = 0.033), indicating rural HEIs may face greater administrative bloat following heightened compliance demands. These findings suggest that rural HEIs may face disproportionate financial strain which could crowd out student investments and community engagement.

articles.title: Do voters want (and reward) stricter political finance regulation? Evidence from South Africa.
articles.authors: Sarah Brierley; Daniel de Kadt
articles.abstract: Efforts to reduce political corruption often focus on stricter regulation of, and enhanced transparency about, political finance. Do voters favor such reforms, and do they reward (and punish) parties that enact (retrench) them? We examine these questions in South Africa, where the ruling African National Congress (ANC) introduced — and later effectively reversed— the Political Party Funding Act (PPFA), which de-anonymized donors and capped contributions. Using a nationally representative survey (N = 1800) with embedded experiments, we measure voter support for such regulations and test how information about the reform and its reversal shapes voter preferences. Although respondents generally express support for tighter regulations, they do not become more favorable toward the ANC after learning about the PPFA. Information about the reversal decreases declared ANC vote intention by around 5 percentage points. Auxiliary tests suggest that voters' doubts about the enforceability of the Act may explain the limited positive updating.

articles.title: Demand Networks and Informal Volunteering
articles.authors: Hjalmar Bang Carlsen; Jonas Toubøl
articles.abstract: Patterns of volunteering have predominantly been explained by focusing on the supply side in terms of volunteers’ resources and motivations. We shift the focus to the demand side of volunteering and develop the concept of demand networks. We argue that experienced demand for help in one’s personal network is important to explain why individuals engage in informally organized voluntary help and support: the amount of demand for help a person experiences in their network influences the likelihood that the person helps. To explain why individuals who perceive similar levels of demand do not all volunteer to the same extent, we theorize how demand networks are mediated by the institutional factors of social values and gender roles. We hypothesize that altruistic values and gendered social roles dispose individuals to respond differently to demands for help, with women and those holding stronger altruistic values being more likely to act on the needs they perceive. We examine the hypotheses using a cross-sectional survey inquiring about informally organized volunteering during COVID-19. The results clearly indicate the importance of the demand side to adequately explain informal volunteering. We argue that our findings imply that sociologists should reconceptualize social connections not only as providing access to resources but also as a source of demands on individuals. In doing so attention should be paid to gender roles which the results suggest function as an amplifier of demand networks association with informal volunteering. We further discuss how the results have implications for building social capital and societal resilience in times of crisis.

articles.title: How Americans Spend their Time Online
articles.authors: David Lazer; Burak Ozturan; Christo Wilson; David Choffnes; Cassidy Waldrip; Lu Hsiu Chi; John Wihbey
articles.abstract:
We examine where people spend their time online, analyzing desktop browsing data collected from the National Internet Observatory (NIO). Key findings include:
● A few platforms dominate where we spend our time. The top 10 platforms captured about half (49%) of all online time, with Gmail at number one with 16.4%.
● A tiny number of companies dominate where we spend time. Most user attention is funneled through a handful of corporations. Alphabet (Google’s parent company) alone accounts for 35% of total browsing time in our sample, followed by Meta (8.9%), Microsoft (5.1%), Yahoo (4.3%), and Amazon (3.0%). These five companies capture more than half of all time Americans spend online on desktop.
● Americans spend half their online time on just two things: social media (25.3%) and email (24.9%).
● AI is already bigger than news. Large Language Model (LLM) tools, such as ChatGPT, now account for 2.9% of total online time, while news is only 2.5%.
● The Web is highly age-segregated. Users over 65 spend 36.7% of their online time on email and 14% on Facebook, versus 11% and 2%, respectively, for users under 30. Older people are still using Yahoo and AOL for email (9%, 2%, respectively), both of which barely register among younger users. The oldest cohort spends 4.7% of their time on news sites, far more than the youngest cohort (1.2%). In contrast, users under 30 spend 13% of their time on YouTube, 9% on Google apps (Docs, Drive, Meet, Classroom, and other Google services excluding Gmail, Search, and YouTube), and 3% on ChatGPT, as compared to 6%, 3%, and <1%, respectively, among the oldest cohort.

articles.title: The Moral Question: Norms and Anti-System Politics
articles.authors: Daniel A. N. Goldstein; Tore Wig
articles.abstract: Although moral norms are often invoked as political guardrails, their measurement and causal influence remain understudied. We theorize the link between moral norms, personal judgments, and attitudinal consequences and test it in a pre-registered survey experiment with financial incentives. Citizens rarely confront democratic violation alone, but rather bundled ``anti-system'' behaviors of potentially unequal moral weight. Respondents faced moral trade-offs concerning political violence, corruption, and anti-democratic actions, with personal scandals as a baseline. Using a second-order approach to elicit beliefs about what others consider morally wrong, we find that norms against democratic violations are descriptively the weakest, and all lag behind norms against violence. Norms primarily shift judgments when respondents face large discrepancies from their initial perceptions and have strong conformity motives, but this largely does not translate into attitudinal shifts. The findings reveal a moral hierarchy among anti-system behaviors, and detail the consequences and limitations of moral norms for politics.

articles.title: Le res novae tra questione operaia e intelligenza artificiale. Un confronto lessicometrico esplorativo tra Rerum novarum (1891) e Magnifica humanitas (2026)
articles.authors: Riccardo Benotti
articles.abstract: A centotrentacinque anni dalla Rerum novarum, la Magnifica humanitas di Leone XIV si apre richiamando le “res novae del nostro tempo” e si colloca esplicitamente nel solco della prima grande enciclica sociale. Il presente contributo, di carattere esplorativo, confronta per via lessicometrica i due testi per descrivere che cosa muti, sul piano del lessico, nel passaggio dalla questione operaia a quella dell’intelligenza artificiale, impiegando keyness con misura dell’effetto, analisi dei campi semantici, ricchezza lessicale e controllo qualitativo mediante concordanze. Emerge una continuità di parte del lessico morale, con frequenze comparabili per giustizia e carità, e un marcato spostamento di enfasi, dal vocabolario di lavoro e proprietà a quello di tecnica, persona, dignità e custodia. La lettura ravvicinata e un corpus di controllo di quattro documenti magisteriali recenti (Laborem exercens, Laudato si’, Fratelli tutti, Antiqua et nova) ridimensionano però l’apparente novità dell’enciclica: il calo del lemma natura non è abbandono del giusnaturalismo, ma variazione di registro; il lessico personalista e tecnologico è eredità del magistero recente che l’enciclica condensa; la sua nota più riconoscibile, la preferenza per il termine custodia riferito alla persona, non corrisponde a un primato del più ampio campo della cura, dove prevale la Laudato si’. Il contributo è soprattutto metodologico: il caso mostra che la lessicometria applicata ai testi magisteriali, senza vaglio qualitativo, genera falsi positivi, e che i conteggi vanno verificati con concordanze, controllo sulle lingue d’origine e un corpus di riferimento.

articles.title: Insta-Famous or Invisible: Social Media Use and Belonging at a Public Flagship University
articles.authors: Katherine Furl
articles.abstract: Social media and U.S. public universities hold as-yet-unrealized potential for equity. Both institutions, however, also serve as reminders of social inequality while normalizing relatively privileged lifestyles. Past scholarship highlights how symbolic capital, felt stigma, and self-inflicted symbolic violence can maintain inequality, yet their operation across interconnected digital and higher educational contexts remains under-analyzed. Through 51 interviews with students at a U.S. public flagship university, I investigate how social media use impacts perceived inequality in higher education. Social media—particularly image-centric platforms prompting users to share visual representations of their offline lives—more readily aided the accumulation of symbolic capital and digital prestige among students better equipped to emulate culturally dominant lifestyle content through proximity to hegemonic norms. The same platforms more readily amplified exposure to felt stigma and experiences with digital non-recognition among students distanced from these norms. Students experiencing felt stigma could exhibit learned invalidation, considering their lives unworthy of certain forms of digital documentation. Further, women students faced greater pressure to document their lives through image-centric platforms. I highlight a cross-institutional context where digital comparisons intertwine with access to perceived-vital resources for social integration and upward mobility, revealing digital platforms’ potential to intensify unequal experiences in higher education.

articles.title: “There’s Always a Way to Get the Story:” Rural Journalism and Resourcefulness at the Periphery
articles.authors: Gregory P Perreault; Celeste González de Bustamante
articles.abstract: US rural journalists face financially precarious circumstances given their lack of resources, which forces many rural journalists to work second jobs to meet their own needs and employ radical resourcefulness in order to meet their communities information needs. Through the lens of journalism at the periphery, the present study explores in-depth interviews with 28 US-based rural journalists in order to understand their experiences with financial precarity and to manifest greater understanding regarding their resource needs.

articles.title: Anthropocene and Empire: Discourse Networks of the Human Record
articles.authors: James Jaehoon Lee; Joshua Beckelhimer
articles.abstract: Scientists have recently proposed 1610 as a candidate for the first year of the new geological epoch known as the Anthropocene, pinpointing the rise of European colonialism and the global movement of life among ecosystems it precipitated as the triggers for measurable changes in the earth system. Using digital humanities methods to mine historical archives, this essay evaluates the relation between colonialism, early modern globalism, and the origins of the Anthropocene. We argue that the Anthropocene was initiated by a premodern earth system that defined life across the globe in spatial terms, furthering the goals of empire — a regime of biopower that has not been adequately acknowledged in debates on the Anthropocene.

articles.title: Wearing Many Hats: How Rural U.S. Newspaper Journalists Negotiate Professional Identity Amid Digital and Economic Disruption
articles.authors: Sayyed Fawad Ali Shah; Teddi A. Joyce; Breann E. Murphy; Ben Cunningham; Gregory P Perreault
articles.abstract: Our study seeks to interrogate how local journalists conceptualize professionalism and negotiate their professional role-identities amid economic and technological disruption. Based on 17 in-depth interviews, we found that journalists idealized journalistic values such as objectivity, accuracy, and community service. However, job insecurity, lack of resources, increased workload, inability of their organizations to keep up with the changing nature of journalism in the emerging digital media landscape, and juggling different responsibilities in their organizations, shaped their professional experiences and routines. Our participants also noted that the traditional separation between editorial and marketing departments in their organizations had evaporated or shrunk, although most viewed collaboration between these departments as necessary for organizational survival rather than a threat to journalistic autonomy. The findings highlight how organizational culture and economic instability are reshaping professional identities and journalistic practices in rural news environments. Based on the findings of our study, we suggest ways in which news organizations, journalism schools, and local press associations could help local newspapers.

articles.title: How Much War Builds a State? Fiscal Bargaining in the Shadow of War
articles.authors: Daniel A. N. Goldstein; Yusuf Magiya
articles.abstract: We present a formal model that examines how external conflict reshapes the bargaining process over fiscal control between a central state and a peripheral elite. Our findings reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between war-related pressures and state fiscal control. Low-to-moderate war pressure enhances state fiscal control by strengthening the state's bargaining power. However, excessive pressure undermines state control. This outcome is influenced by the degree to which the interests of the state and the elites align. We also identify instances when states fall into a `capacity trap,' where those with low initial fiscal control sacrifice future revenues to finance ongoing conflict. Using historical fiscal revenue data from Europe and case studies of Ancien Régime France and the Ottoman Empire, we test the predictions and find supporting evidence. These findings refine bellicist theory by highlighting the contingent benefits of conflict on state development when accounting for the complexities involved in state financing.

articles.title: Dynamic Climate Risk and the Vulnerability Ratchet
articles.authors: Michael Weisberg; Koko Warner; Zinta Zommers; Youssef Nassef; Simon Levin; Erol Akcay
articles.abstract: Changing climate poses increasing risk to communities worldwide. Climate risk is a complex phenomenon that emerges from the interaction of physical, biological, and social systems. The dominant framework for assessing climate risk, developed across successive IPCC assessments, focuses on hazard, vulnerability, and exposure as contributing components of climate risk. This framework has organized research and policy productively, but it remains limited as it represents these components separate inputs evaluated at a single point in time. As a snapshot, it cannot capture path dependence, compounding, or irreversibility, the properties that make climate risk most difficult to address. To address this limitation, we introduce a Dynamic Climate Risk (DCR) framework that makes the coupling between risk components explicit and tracks their co-evolution over time. Analyzing the hazard–vulnerability coupling, we show that when hazard events outpace recovery, vulnerability fails to return to baseline and instead drifts upward in a self-reinforcing “vulnerability ratchet.” We derive the threshold event frequency at which the ratchet engages, and a lock-in vulnerability beyond which recovery capacity collapses, defining a finite policy window whose length we bound analytically. Mitigation remains essential over the long run, but because hazard is effectively fixed on near-term policy horizons while vulnerability and exposure are not, the most consequential near-term choices concern managing these couplings rather than emissions alone. We illustrate the framework with three cases, Bangladesh, the 2022 Pakistan floods, and the divergent trajectories of Haiti and Cuba, each exercising different parts of its structure.

articles.title: Youth Unemployment and Mismatch in the Turkish Labour Market
articles.authors: Mustafa Mert Ozyilmaz
articles.abstract:
This paper analyses youth unemployment and education–job mismatch in
Turkey using individual-level data from the Turkish Statistical Institute(TÜİK)
Labour Force Statistics for 2015. The youth (15–24) unemployment rate stands
at 18.5%, more than double the adult (25–64) rate of 8.8%, with a pronounced
gender gap: female youth face a 22.2% unemployment rate against 16.5%
for males. Unemployment is highest among college-educated youth (29.5%),
alongside high labour-force participation (75.1%) in this group. We construct
two qualification-mismatch indicators for employed youth. Vertical mismatch -
education level relative to the occupational modal - affects 53% of employed
college graduates and 49% of vocational high school graduates, who work in
occupations where the typical worker has lower formal education. Horizontal
mismatch, field of education relative to occupation, is estimable for the
